ACL 重建後不敢變向：如何分清膝不穩、任務恐懼與回場意願？ 
回到任何運動、回到高風險運動與恢復原有層級，會得到不同的成功率。本月串接 500 名年輕患者的回場分析與 21 位治療師的心理照護經驗，建立「先確認目標與穩定性，再分級接觸害怕任務」的執行流程，並保留心理支持療效、性別差異與個人放行條件的不確定性。 
sport-medicine 
assessment 
training 
monitoring 
ACL 重建後，當運動員的身體檢測、膝部信心與變向意願不同步，團隊如何判斷應先重評膝穩定性、安排分級任務、轉介心理專業，或重新協商運動目標？ 
以回場結果的觀察關聯界定需要評估的領域，再以質性研究補上溝通與執行方式。兩篇均已依所附全文閱讀方法、結果、表格、討論及限制；它們沒有直接驗證心理介入療效、性別專屬處方或安全回場切點。本文的證據分級是編輯對本問題的判讀，並非沿用原試驗的手術證據等級。 
2026 年 10 月的 ACL 心理準備決定因素與青少年髕骨穩定手術心理準備題名，顯示傷後心理準備持續受到關注；本封包 ACL／膝關節亦有 14 筆受控題名訊號。這些只說明選題時機。 
既有第 37 週已介紹多面向回場，第 40 週與第 43 週分別整理心理支持及回場定義；尚缺少把「想不想回、敢不敢做、膝是否穩、支持能否取得」串成不同處置路徑的深入方案。 
實務容易將遲疑統稱為心理問題，或以力量進步催促回場。現在需要把關節疑慮、具體任務恐懼、外界壓力與自主選擇分開，讓每次進階有負責人、實際劑量及複評理由。 
分辨研究的三種回場結果，以及臨床參與連續性與實際競技表現的差別。 
正確解讀 OR、信心單題與膝穩定性的關聯，不將它們變成因果效果或個人通關值。 
建立包含身體能力、具體恐懼、意願與照護資源的評估紀錄。 
依個人反應執行分級任務，明確記錄進階、退階、停止及轉介條件。 
回場遲疑可能同時包含關節症狀、能力不足、再傷恐懼、生活優先順序與資源障礙。評估先問運動員希望回到什麼，再查目前允許與實際完成的任務。信心、穩定性、功能與意願各提供一部分資訊；兩篇來源都不足以產生可自動放行的總分。 
RTP、RTHR 與 RTA 
本研究 RTP 指回到傷前高風險運動及層級；RTHR 指回到任何層級的跳躍、旋轉或切入運動；RTA 指回到任何運動，包含跑步、游泳等較低風險活動。 
【source-stated】研究 RTP 是自報運動種類與層級的分類，未直接測量球速、比賽效率或持續競爭能力；不能當作已客觀恢復表現。 
source-stated 
心理準備 
恢復專項活動時的心理準備，包含認知評估、情緒反應與行為準備。 
【cross-source-synthesis】敢做動作、希望回場及身體能承受動作是不同問題；低意願也可能是知情選擇。 
cross-source-synthesis 
治療聯盟 
患者與治療師對共同目標、任務及信任關係形成的合作。 
【source-stated】治療師認為自己提供支持，不保證運動員感受到相同支持；須直接詢問本人。 
分級暴露 
依患者反應，逐步重新接觸害怕的專項動作或情境。 
【mixed】本期提供治療師經驗，沒有建立固定組次、有效療程或安全進階分數。任務仍須符合醫療與功能限制。 
mixed 
膝部信心單題 
回場分析使用 ACL-QOL 第 30 題，0 表示嚴重受缺乏信心困擾，100 表示完全不受困擾。 
【source-stated】它是心理準備的替代指標，並非 ACL-RSI，也未建立可用於放行的分數。 
勝算比 OR 
比較結果發生相對於未發生之勝算的比值。 
【cross-source-synthesis】女性 OR 0.47 不能改寫為女性回場機率只有男性的 47%；信心每分的 OR 也不能直接換算成回場機率增加百分比。 
研究中的臨床不穩定 
任一追蹤有至少第 2 級 pivot-shift，或多次追蹤有第 1 級 pivot-shift，歸為臨床不穩定。 
【source-stated】這是受訓臨床人員在多次追蹤中的研究分類；單次正常結果或本人沒有滑脫感，均不能自行重建此分類或作回場許可。 
功能里程碑可能建立掌握感 
受訪治療師描述，將可完成的小目標連到專項需求，可讓患者理解身體進步並累積信心。研究沒有測試掌握感是否中介回場效果。 
【mixed】每個任務都說明目的，完成後同時討論動作品質與本人經驗；不只告知測驗分數。 
pmid-42781749 
穩定性與信心可能相互影響，方向尚未確立 
回場分析中，膝穩定性及信心與部分回場結果有關；然而沒有介入操弄或足以確立中介路徑的分析，不能確定改善其中一項便會造成另一項或回場率上升。 
【cross-source-synthesis】對遲疑同時評估身體與心理，不預先將原因歸入單一領域。 
pmid-42865115 
社會情境可能促進或阻礙參與 
治療師描述同儕支持、社會比較及家長教練壓力的雙面作用；回場分析未充分量測性別化環境、照護可近性與持續意願。 
【mixed】保留私下對話及目標重談的空間，記錄資源障礙，避免由性別推定個人心理特質。 
225/494（45.5%） 
兩年內回到傷前高風險運動與層級 
14–25 歲高再傷風險 ACL 重建分析；屬研究 RTP 定義，並非直接競賽表現測量。

心理照護質性研究的資料來源 
荷蘭 11 位、挪威 10 位治療師；142 頁逐字稿，形成四個主題。這些不是患者數、療程劑量或療效。 
STABILITY 1 多中心手術隨機試驗的回溯次級分析；本題的性別、信心與回場關聯屬觀察性分析，不能因母試驗隨機化而視為因果試驗。 
500 名傷前參與跳躍、旋轉或切入運動的患者，14–25 歲、骨骼成熟，平均 18.8 ± 3.2 歲；234 男、266 女。母試驗要求符合指定高再傷風險特徵，手術為腿後肌自體移植物 ACL 重建加或不加 LET。 
術後 3、6、12、24 個月追蹤，記錄兩年內三種回場結果。以多變項邏輯斯迴歸及向後選模分析術前／術中因素，敏感度模型加入 ACL-QOL 信心單題及多次 pivot-shift 分類。信心通常取 12 個月；較早回場者取回場前一次訪視。傷前層級因共線性移除，運動種類未納入模型。 
三種回場結果 
RTP 225/494（45.5%）；RTHR 380/497（76.5%）；RTA 430/497（86.5%）。 
術後兩年內，各結果使用可用資料分母；不是同一時間點的能力檢測。

女性相較男性；敏感度模型 pseudo R² = 0.07。模型未成為可靠個人預測器。

信心每分 OR 1.01（95% CI 1.00–1.02），p = 0.04；穩定膝 OR 2.58（1.41–4.72），p < 0.01。 
女性敏感度模型 n = 252，pseudo R² = 0.09；信心為替代單題，區間依原文四捨五入。

手術時間與女性 RTHR 
受傷至手術 ≤3 個月相較 >3 個月，OR 2.96（95% CI 1.59–5.51），p < 0.01。 
女性敏感度模型 n = 252；時間分類是分析條件，不能轉成普遍手術期限。 
表 5；Discussion 
其他回場定義的性別結果 
性別不是 RTP 的顯著預測因子；RTA 敏感度模型女性 OR 0.67（95% CI 0.33–1.36），p = 0.27。 
RTP 與 RTA 敏感度模型分別 n = 457、444；不能把 RTHR 差異概括到所有回場結果。 
表 4；Return to Performance；Return to Any Sport 
【cross-source-synthesis】研究最有用的進展是界定結果：回到任何運動不能代表回到原有層級，女性 RTHR 關聯值得檢查照護與支持需求。信心及穩定性提供評估方向，但低模型擬合、替代心理測量及未測環境因素，限制個人預測與因果推論。提高回場率必須以本人希望回場為前提。 
排除四名術後六個月前移植物斷裂者；結果不能代表所有手術患者。 
母試驗 618 人，傷前高風險運動 525 人，最終分析 500 人；各模型另有缺失及離群值排除。 
男性 RTHR／RTA 可用分母在正文列值與整體總數不完全相容；女性表列 190 人與 72.0%、223 人與 84.5%亦有分母疑點，本文不採性別原始比例作圖。 
沒有專門心理準備量表，未持續確認每位患者是否仍以各回場結果為目標。 
性別次群一組顯著、另一組不顯著，不能單獨證明兩組效應不同；缺乏充分交互作用驗證。 
手術時間可能受到可近性、功能與生活安排影響；不能據關聯要求提早手術或選擇 LET。 
部分作者揭露研究資助、顧問及權利金關係，需與方法限制一併閱讀。

半結構式焦點團體質性研究，以系統性文本濃縮分析整理經驗；作者標示 Level 5。 
透過研究團隊專業網絡策略性招募 21 位具 ACL 重建復健經驗的治療師，荷蘭 11 位、挪威 10 位；不是患者介入樣本。 
2024 年 3–10 月兩國各進行三場視訊焦點團體，錄音逐字轉錄。訪綱經運動心理專業諮詢及翻譯；兩國分別分析初步意義單位與濃縮內容，再共同形成主題，持續討論研究者預設立場。 
招募 
聯繫 33 位，7 位婉拒、5 位未回覆，納入 21 位。 
策略性網絡招募，不能視為一般治療師的代表性盛行率調查。 
Participants and Recruitment 
治療師經驗 
荷蘭中位數 17 年（範圍 8–25），挪威 19 年（9–25）。 
分別 n = 11、10；不是心理治療訓練年資。

四主題涵蓋治療聯盟、心理準備與動機策略、內外在影響、治療師角色。

Does the Benefit Last? 
Following supplements, training loads and symptoms through the whole task 
Ying and Bing discuss eight studies asking whether early gains, improved sensations or better laboratory numbers translate into the outcomes people actually need. They examine repeated judo efforts, menthol and running, ketone precursors, protein, resistance training and breast injury surveillance while preserving uncertainty and practical limits.

Distinguish early benefits from performance across the complete target task. 
Separate sensations, biochemical exposure, physical capacity and functional outcomes. 
Interpret uncertain differences without claiming equivalence or individual response. 
Recognize how disclosure and follow-up affect injury surveillance. 
Identify what evidence would support retaining, revising or withdrawing a strategy. 
Brand pronunciation: edgeSport4Podcast is spoken as Edge Sport for Podcast. 
All research discussion is based exclusively on the supplied weeklyReport for 2026-w45. 
The integrated monitoring approach discussed at the end is an unvalidated EDGE SPORT educational proposal. 
Consult the written weekly report and its original sources for full methods, confidence intervals and unresolved reporting discrepancies. 
Judo supplementation: pmid-42905127. Menthol running trial: pmid-42922437. Mountain bike BDO trial: pmid-42852530. 
Protein source review: pmid-42954267. Whey biomarker trial: pmid-42929456. 
Older adult load prescription: pmid-42954324. Flywheel calf raises: pmid-42831264. Women's rugby breast injury surveillance: pmid-42960524. 
A good start, then what? 
Repeated judo efforts reveal why an early benefit cannot stand in for the whole day. 
Feeling better and measuring exposure 
Menthol and BDO separate sensations and biochemical changes from the outcomes they might promise. 
Protein and the comparison that matters 
Protein source uncertainty and whey biomarker results require careful comparisons. 
Choosing a load and checking transfer 
Older adult training and acute flywheel responses show different kinds of task specificity. 
What the injury record misses 
Breast injury surveillance highlights disclosure, denominators and follow-up. 
A decision people can revisit 
The hosts assemble an explicitly unvalidated practical approach and close with actionable questions. 
You know that hopeful feeling when a new strategy works in the first session? Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and this week's question is whether that benefit survives the whole task, including the part when you're tired and nobody's watching closely. 
warm 
And I'm Bing. Here on edgeSport4Podcast, I'd like us to stay with that tired person for a while. If the opening rounds look better but the later rounds slip, what would actually persuade us to keep the strategy? 
curious 
The judo study makes that question concrete. Thirty-five competitive athletes completed a randomized crossover comparison of caffeine, beetroot juice, their combination and placebo during a simulated competition day. They had low habitual caffeine intake, which already narrows who this tells us about. 
clear 
And simulated competition needs unpacking. Were they fighting actual tournament matches, or repeating something more controlled across the day? 
They combined practice bouts with a special judo fitness test that counts throws, then added another test after recovery. Compared with placebo, caffeine produced about one extra throw in the first test. By the fifth test, it produced about half a throw fewer. 
So an opening advantage changed direction later. That's more useful than one average across the day, but half a throw is a group estimate. How confident should a coach be that it identifies what happened to one athlete? 
reflective 
Quite cautious. The authors said none of the condition differences exceeded their model's minimum detectable change at 95 percent confidence. 
cautious 
That limits individual verdicts. Also, this wasn't one caffeine serving before breakfast and nothing else. The study gave three milligrams per kilogram twice, before exercise and after the third bout. We shouldn't accidentally describe that as the total daily amount. 
Exactly, and blood caffeine remained elevated later, so running out of circulating caffeine isn't a supported explanation. Beetroot alone and the combination had more favorable fifth-test throw counts than placebo. Would you call the combination the obvious winner? 
I wouldn't. Beetroot alone did better on some later fitness-index results than the combination. That index also includes heart rate, which caffeine can raise. I'd want the separate outcomes and later rounds before deciding what the apparent win actually means. 
That makes me think about another kind of apparent win. If running feels less uncomfortable, that matters to the runner. But what else needs to change before we say the strategy improved their breathing or their performance? 
The menthol trial separates those questions nicely. Trained runners wore a mask with a menthol preparation near the chin or a strawberry-scented comparison. At 85 percent of peak treadmill speed, average time to exhaustion was 445 seconds with menthol and 406 with the comparison. 
About 39 seconds longer sounds attractive. Was that everyone who entered, and was it a race against the clock? 
Neither. The analysis included 18 runners after three were excluded for outlying changes in exhaustion time. Running until you stop is also different from completing a fixed race distance, so that extra time doesn't translate directly into a race improvement. 
And the runners knew which sensation they were getting. Positive expectations were greater with menthol, although the difference remained after statistical adjustment. Breathlessness fell during exercise, while the main measured heart and lung responses showed no condition differences, including oxygen uptake and oxygen saturation. 
So the feeling deserves attention without becoming proof of improved oxygenation. Would the result change your advice about how to use menthol? 
It wouldn't justify improvising a delivery method. This was a specific mask preparation in healthy runners, without evidence here for respiratory disease or heat. Even the 42-second measurement error discussed by the authors came from another study, so it isn't a personal pass mark. 
That same separation helps with BDO, a ketone precursor tested during an eight-day mountain bike race. Among 18 finishers, post-stage blood beta-hydroxybutyrate averaged about 1.02 millimolar with BDO and 0.37 with control. The supplement clearly changed that measured exposure. 
But did the riders recover better, sleep better or maintain cognition better once that blood number moved? 
No advantage was confirmed for those measured outcomes or heart-rate trajectories. Only finishers were analyzed, both withdrawals were in the BDO group, and the control wasn't calorie matched. It's a useful finding about this strategy, with limited grounds for judging every ketone product. 
Which brings us to a quieter purchasing decision. Someone starting resistance training asks whether plant protein can replace whey. The review pooled five randomized trials, but its outcomes were lean mass and fat mass. It wasn't a comprehensive test of strength or sporting performance. 
And no clear difference in those outcomes still leaves a question. How wide was the range of plausible differences? 
For lean mass, plant minus whey was minus 0.35, with a confidence interval from minus 2.46 to plus 1.76. The supplied extraction doesn't clearly label the mass unit, so we won't add one. That interval leaves substantial uncertainty about the difference. 
Then calling them equivalent would outrun the design. There's also a denominator trap here. The review describes 372 participants across included studies, but the lean-mass comparison actually contained 88 receiving plant protein and 93 receiving whey. Those are different counts answering different questions. 
Yes, and soy, pea and chia shouldn't become one interchangeable product. Formulations varied, and chia had only one study. For a beginner choosing something sustainable, preferences and the existing diet belong in the conversation, with no promise of an identical muscle gain. 
Existing diet matters in the other whey trial too. Fifty-nine male track-and-field athletes received whey or carbohydrate control for eight weeks, but their usual protein intake wasn't quantified. The clearer intervention signals were in the enzymes ALT and AST, rather than every recovery marker. 
When you say clearer, do you mean the whey groups improved, or their changes differed from the control groups? 
Their changes differed from control. CK and CRP had some within-group decreases, but their treatment comparisons weren't statistically significant. Only ALT showed a significant additional difference by training type, with p equal to 0.003. Without performance testing, these results don't authorize more training. 
That distinction between a measured change and a useful next step follows us into load selection. In the older adult trial, researchers classified high-functioning community adults as having a velocity deficit. Does that label sound more diagnostic than the evidence allows? 
It does. This was a research classification from a force-velocity profile, estimating the relationship between force and movement speed. The theoretical endpoints are extrapolated values. The classification rule wasn't a validated diagnosis, and these participants don't represent all older adults. 
So did prescribing the supposedly matching load produce better function than deliberately choosing the other load? 
No extra functional benefit was confirmed after twelve weeks. The lower-load approach favored the estimated speed endpoint, while the higher-load approach favored force. Maximum power rose by about 32 watts and 36 watts respectively, but the difference between those changes remained uncertain. 
The estimated power difference was minus 3.7 watts, with a confidence interval from minus 20.6 to plus 13.1. So different adaptations didn't establish a better overall option. There was also no non-exercising control, which limits what those improvements alone can tell us. 
Would you still measure the profile, then? Or does this make the extra testing hard to justify? 
I'd ask what decision it will change. It can describe adaptation, but this trial doesn't support automatically replacing a suitable program because of one classification. Ability, preference and functional goals still matter, especially when the sample was high functioning and the analysis wasn't fully intention to treat. 
And a suitable load can depend on when you test. In 37 male national-level jumpers, researchers compared three flywheel calf-raise inertias. Four minutes after three sets of eight, medium inertia produced an average jump-height increase of 1.55 centimeters from baseline. 
Light inertia increased height by 0.80 centimeters, while the high-inertia change was uncertain. Medium also performed better on reactive strength index, here defined as jump height divided by ground contact time. That formula matters when comparing results from different testing systems. 
And four minutes is the only post-exercise window they measured. There was no resting control, and equal repetitions didn't mean equal mechanical work. I'd test a proposed warm-up against the actual jumping task before extending this to competition, long-term gains or injury prevention. 
That need to check the actual outcome also changes how we read injury records. In women's rugby, the breast injury study compared clinical surveillance with an anonymous retrospective survey. Both captured injuries that could exist while someone continued playing, which makes absence an incomplete measure. 
The clinical records contained three injuries across 1,204 match hours, or 2.5 per thousand hours. The retrospective estimate was 28.5 per thousand. That's a striking gap, but these were independently recruited groups with different observation periods and exposure estimates. 
So we can't say the medical system missed exactly eleven out of every twelve injuries. What else complicates that comparison? 
The retrospective numerator is described as both 144 injuries and 144 people with at least one injury. Repeated events aren't fully reconstructed. Several other counts and percentages also conflict, so the report keeps the main recording gap while resisting a precise estimate of the true burden. 
The follow-up gap feels just as consequential. Of the three prospectively recorded injuries, only one received a physical assessment, and none had a follow-up physical assessment. Players continued participating, but that doesn't tell us that pain or interference with performance had resolved. 
And a form can't guarantee a conversation. Education and a breast-specific reporting field were already present. Private reporting and reliable clinical follow-up are reasonable directions, but this study didn't isolate which process would improve disclosure. We should ask athletes what makes speaking up possible. 
Then our practical proposal needs room for both performance and conversation. Before changing anything, name the task, the time window and the outcome that would matter to the person. This integrated EDGE SPORT approach is educational and hasn't been validated as a complete decision system. 
I'd add the actual exposure and a fair comparison. Record what was taken or lifted, the rest periods and the surrounding conditions. What would change your decision if the early result looked good but the later result or symptoms looked worse? 
I'd revisit or withdraw the added strategy rather than let the opening gain settle the question. Agree on that review beforehand, include private symptom reporting and arrange appropriate assessment when needed. We aren't offering a universal dose, stopping threshold or individual medical clearance. 
encouraging 
And keep the person's goal in view when deciding whether the benefit is worth the effort. Name the outcome, check the whole task and follow up on symptoms. Thanks for joining us. The written weekly report and original sources hold the methods and uncertainties behind today's conversation. 
In 35 judo athletes, caffeine versus placebo increased first-test throws by 1.06, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.60 to 1.52, but reduced fifth-test throws by 0.57, with an interval of -1.14 to -0.005. 
Controlled simulated competition in low habitual caffeine consumers. Caffeine was administered at 3 mg/kg twice. No condition difference exceeded the model MDC95, limiting individual interpretation. Later blood caffeine remained elevated, without establishing the mechanism of declining performance. 
Menthol increased modeled treadmill time to exhaustion by 39.4 seconds, with a 95% confidence interval of 12.3 to 66.4. Condition means were 445 and 406 seconds. 
Eighteen analyzed runners after three outlier exclusions. Participants were not blinded. The expectation-adjusted difference was 32.9 seconds. The task was not a race time trial, and the external 42-second typical error is not an individual benefit threshold. No improved oxygenation or disease treatment was established. 
Among 18 mountain bike race finishers, post-stage beta-hydroxybutyrate estimated marginal means were 1.02 mM with BDO and 0.37 mM with control, without confirmed advantages in measured recovery, cognition, sleep or heart-rate trajectories. 
BDO had eight analyzed finishers and control ten. Both withdrawals were in the BDO group. The control was not calorie matched. Findings concern this formulation, schedule and small completer sample. 
The plant-minus-whey lean-mass pooled mean difference was -0.35, with a 95% confidence interval of -2.46 to 1.76. 
The supplied extraction does not clearly identify the estimate's mass unit. The lean-mass forest plot compares 88 plant and 93 whey participants, rather than all 372 people described across included studies. Five trials in untrained adults do not establish equivalence, uniform effects across plant sources or competitive performance effects. 
In the eight-week trial of 59 male athletes, ALT and AST showed significant time-by-supplement interactions. Only ALT showed a significant time-by-supplement-by-training-type interaction, p = 0.003. 
CK and CRP time-by-supplement interactions were not significant, p = 0.082 and p = 0.090. Within-group decreases do not establish treatment superiority. Usual protein intake was not quantified, and no direct performance outcome or liver-protection effect was established. 
At twelve weeks, maximum power increased by 32.0 W in the matched-load group and 35.7 W in the comparison group. The between-group change difference was -3.7 W, with a 95% confidence interval of -20.6 to 13.1, p = 0.660. 
High-functioning community older adults meeting a study-specific velocity-deficit classification. Different force and velocity adaptations did not establish superior function or equivalent programs. There was no non-exercising control, and analysis was not fully intention to treat. 
Four minutes after flywheel calf raises, mean jump-height changes were 1.55 cm with medium inertia, 0.80 cm with light inertia and 0.38 cm with high inertia. 
Thirty-seven male national-level jumpers completed three sets of eight. Medium-inertia change had a 95% confidence interval of 1.08 to 2.02 cm. High-inertia change was uncertain. No non-exercise control, other post-exercise windows or matched mechanical work were available. RSI was jump height divided by contact time. 
Breast injury recording rates were 2.5 per 1,000 match hours prospectively and 28.5 retrospectively, based on three records across 1,204 hours and an author-used numerator of 144 across 5,055 hours. 
Independent cohorts, different periods and estimated retrospective exposure prevent interpreting the reported rate ratio of 11.4 as a true underreporting multiplier. The retrospective numerator mixes injured people and events. Only one prospective injury received a physical assessment and none received follow-up physical assessment. 
Predefining task outcomes, comparing the full time window and reviewing exposure, tolerability and symptom disclosure is an EDGE SPORT operational proposal. 
The integrated process is not validated as a complete intervention or decision system and supplies no universal doses, clinical thresholds or return-to-play clearance. 
Define the outcome and time window before adding a strategy. 
Check later performance alongside early gains. 
Keep sensations, biomarkers and functional outcomes distinct. 
Treat uncertain differences as uncertainty rather than equivalence. 
Invite private symptom disclosure and complete appropriate follow-up. 
Use the written weekly report and original sources to review methods and limitations. 
This episode uses synthetic speech. Ying is locally generated from the supplied female-voice sample, and Bing is locally generated from the supplied male-voice sample. The script is prepared by Codex. The episode is educational and does not provide individualized medical advice or return-to-play clearance.

咖啡因前段有效、後段失速：補充與負荷策略如何驗證整段表現？ 
本週八篇研究把決策焦點推向「效益能維持多久、是否轉移到目標任務」：柔道咖啡因、飛輪慣量與高齡力量—速度處方，都呈現明顯的時間或結果特異性。蛋白質、酮體與薄荷醇研究也提醒，體組成、生化變化、感受改善與實際功能必須分開驗證；女子橄欖球乳房傷害則顯示，持續出賽與醫療紀錄稀少，可能掩蓋尚未被辨識的負擔。 
團隊如何在加入補充品或調整阻力負荷前，確認策略改善整段目標任務，並同步追蹤耐受、症狀與漏報？ 
本期共八篇，全部為 full-text-open；full-text-web、full-text-local、full-text-excerpt 與 abstract-only 均為零。已依提供的完整內嵌全文、表格、圖說及可用補充說明整理；僅列名而未提供內容的補充檔不視為已取得數據。全文可支持設計與統計層次的查核，但小樣本、缺乏非運動對照、完成者分析及若干報告不一致，仍限制等效、機轉與個人處方推論。

本研究包以 European Journal of Sport Science 六篇為主，涵蓋補充策略、急性反應肌力及女性傷害監測；Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition 補上蛋白來源統合，Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 則檢驗高齡個人化負荷。共同進展是直接比較策略在特定任務與時間窗的效果；沒有形成跨族群通用方案。柔道與飛輪研究呈現條件間差異，高齡處方與 BDO 研究則未確認預期的功能優勢，兩者並不互相矛盾。

A Green Score, and Then What? 
Turning training plans and recovery signals into decisions worth checking 
Ying and Bing examine eight sources on weekly soccer workloads, endurance readiness, caffeine expectations, pre-sleep nutrition, beetroot juice, adolescent hip injury, women's soccer ACL surveillance and cannabinoid communication. They ask what would actually justify changing the next session while keeping measured outcomes, clinical decisions and an unvalidated EDGE SPORT monitoring proposal distinct.

Distinguish workload descriptions and fatigue monitoring from evidence predicting the next task. 
Interpret nutrition and expectation findings using their actual comparisons, outcomes and analysis populations. 
Keep clinical assessment, exposure-adjusted injury surveillance and product communication within their evidence boundaries. 
Describe a traceable training decision without inventing universal scores, progression percentages or clearance rules. 
The written brand edgeSport4Podcast is spoken as Edge Sport for Podcast. 
All research claims derive from the supplied 2026-w44 weekly report. No additional research or historical issue claims are introduced. 
Male soccer workload review: pmid-42627171. Only 2 of 43 studies used dedicated performance tests. 
Endurance readiness review: pmid-42926133. Reported 14 studies and 418 participants with inconsistent age eligibility and tool counts. 
Caffeine expectation meta-analysis: pmid-42897966. Deceptive caffeine-free treatments were compared with baseline, not actual caffeine. 
Pre-sleep nutrition crossover trial: pmid-42897977. Twenty-one female collegiate athletes completed four conditions with three nights per condition. 
Beetroot juice crossover trial: pmid-42899516. Principal inference used 13 female volleyball players who completed both periods. 
Adolescent iliopsoas avulsion report and review: pmid-42925088. Case-level evidence cannot establish treatment superiority or personal clearance dates. The written report flags unresolved reporting discrepancies including injury side and rehabilitation chronology to unrestricted return at three months, so that return date is not presented here as a recovery target or clearance rule. The six-month imaging finding is retained only as a separate case observation about imaging and function, not as validation of the reported return chronology or of individual clearance criteria. Source claims about return timing and clearance remain unverified pending editorial review, and editorReview remains unapproved until those issues are resolved against the original source material. Other discrepancies include youth soccer sample counts and cannabinoid survey collection dates; consult the written report and original sources before publication or implementation. The supplied report records full-text access, but this script does not independently resolve these discrepancies, verify the original sources, or constitute publication approval; the episode remains an unapproved draft pending editorial verification. No clinical recommendation should be inferred from the unresolved chronology or from the isolated imaging observation, and no universal return timeline is supplied by this episode. The clinical action discussed is assessment of concerning symptoms, with activity decisions reserved for the treating team rather than a podcast, readiness score or case-report date. The monitoring workflow is likewise an educational proposal that has not been validated as a complete system, an injury predictor or a medical clearance process. No automatic threshold, dose, progression percentage or recovery deadline is endorsed. Nutrition exposures and follow-up times are study descriptions only. Read the report and original sources for complete methods and limitations before interpreting any quantitative result outside the conversation. The dialogue deliberately separates the meaning of a measurement from the decision it might inform, and repeated local observation is described as reviewable practice rather than proof of causality or established predictive accuracy. No external evidence, current regulatory guidance or personalized advice is added. Synthetic speech disclosure is provided in the episode metadata. Publication approval requires a human evidence review and resolution of material source inconsistencies; the empty verification fields are intentional and should remain empty until that review occurs. This draft is educational and does not diagnose listeners or clear athletes to return to play. All eight research sources are included with claim-level evidence IDs. Quantitative findings retain the source population, comparison and relevant uncertainty where discussed, and the fact-check section preserves the main evidence boundaries. The case's reported unrestricted return date is omitted from the spoken dialogue because the report explicitly identifies a chronology issue. The episode does not infer that symptom resolution alone establishes readiness, nor that persistent imaging findings alone determine restriction. Those questions require individualized clinical interpretation. The same distinction applies to the nutrition and readiness sources, where better scores, comfort or a single functional result do not establish universal capacity for the next task. The practical proposal asks teams to record what they intended, what they changed and what followed, while preserving uncertainty and the athlete's account. This proposal should not be advertised as proven prevention or a validated algorithm. The written report remains the sole source of truth for this draft. 
The score and the session 
A familiar morning dilemma leads to the distinction between workload patterns, fatigue and readiness for a specific task. 
Expectations and bedtime nutrition 
The speakers unpack baseline comparisons, low-certainty expectation effects and a short nutrition trial without detected sleep differences. 
A better jump means what? 
Selective beetroot juice findings show why timing, task and analysis population matter. 
Symptoms, images and denominators 
A rare adolescent hip injury and women's soccer ACL surveillance require different kinds of interpretation. 
The conversation behind the data 
Cannabinoid survey findings lead into a practical, explicitly unvalidated approach to recording and reviewing decisions. 
You've slept badly, your watch looks cheerful, and tomorrow's hard session is already on the board. Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast, I'm Ying, and this week's question is what would actually justify keeping that session, changing it, or asking for an assessment? 
warm 
And I'm Bing, here on edgeSport4Podcast with a coffee and some sympathy for whoever has to make that call. I'd want to know what tomorrow asks of the athlete before deciding how much authority to give today's score. 
That gives us somewhere concrete to begin. The male soccer review found a familiar pattern of recovery after matches, heavier work around the middle of the week and less work before the next match, but familiarity doesn't establish the best arrangement. 
clear 
How often did those studies actually test whether players performed better, rather than simply describe what the week looked like? 
curious 
Only two of the 43 studies used dedicated performance tests. Most of this literature tells us how training was distributed, so it gives a useful map of practice with much less direct evidence about which arrangement improves performance. 
Then I'd keep the map but loosen my attachment to it. If a team wins after a lighter week, the opponent and tactical plan still matter, and coaches might already have changed training because of the opponent they expected. 
reflective 
Exactly, and we need to separate the work from the response. External load is what someone does, such as distance or accelerations, while internal load is their physiological or perceived response, so the same distance doesn't tell the whole story. 
That makes the morning score more interesting, but also more demanding. Is it describing yesterday's cost or tomorrow's capability? 
The endurance readiness review asks essentially that question across a reported 14 studies and 418 participants. Many tools came from fatigue, recovery or adaptation monitoring, and being sensitive to those states doesn't establish that they predict the quality of the next session. 
And that total needs care because the review includes an adolescent swimming subgroup despite adult eligibility criteria, alongside inconsistent tool counts. Ying, how would you explain readiness without making it sound like a quality someone either possesses or lacks? 
I'd describe it as a temporary capacity to handle and effectively complete the next physical and cognitive task. That keeps the task in view, and the authors' framework for combining subjective, physiological, functional and contextual information still needs prospective validation. 
So a useful question becomes whether the information helps us judge a specified session, with its actual quality checked afterward. 
Yes, and perceived readiness brings us to expectations. The caffeine review pooled studies where people received something caffeine-free but were told it contained caffeine, comparing their performance with baseline conditions rather than directly comparing the treatment with real caffeine. 
That comparison matters before any number arrives. What was the average signal, and how much confidence should we place in it? 
Across 17 studies and 257 people, the pooled standardized effect was 0.49, with a confidence interval from 0.28 to 0.69. That's a result expressed on a common statistical scale across different tasks, rather than a percentage improvement. 
And it doesn't tell us how much of real caffeine's effect comes from expectation. The certainty was low, none of the studies had low risk of bias, and particular outcomes such as power didn't show a consistent benefit. 
cautious 
Given that uncertainty, would you still ask an athlete what they expect a recovery strategy to do for them? 
I would, because it helps us interpret their experience while keeping our explanation honest. The review explicitly opposes deceptive administration in practice, so we can record expectations and use consistent encouragement without pretending a product contains something it doesn't. 
That honesty also matters at bedtime, when someone wants reassurance about eating late. In a randomized, blinded crossover trial, 21 female collegiate athletes completed four conditions, receiving casein, an alpha-lactalbumin formula, carbohydrate or placebo for three nights each. 
They didn't detect differences in sleep or perceived recovery between conditions. Does that give us reassurance without establishing a special sleep benefit? 
That's a fair reading within this short study of supported collegiate athletes. It wasn't designed to establish equivalence, sleep was assessed with a wearable, and the findings don't establish long-term effects or treatment benefits for people with insomnia. 
Then the starting question is whether evening food serves an actual nutritional need, with sleep and tolerance followed individually. Those three-night conditions don't supply a universal bedtime prescription, and the study didn't directly measure muscle protein synthesis or competition performance. 
Following the outcome you actually want becomes especially useful with the beetroot juice trial. Female volleyball players completed a demanding jumping protocol, then received beetroot juice or a sea buckthorn control drink in a crossover design, with follow-up through 72 hours. 
Before we call that recovery, which capability improved, and which athletes actually contributed to the main statistical comparison? 
The main model used 13 players who completed both periods. At 72 hours, the estimated advantage in countermovement jump height was 1.5 centimeters, with a confidence interval from 0.05 to 2.97 centimeters, compared with the control drink. 
That's a fairly wide interval, and the overall interaction between condition and time didn't meet the study's significance standard. I'd describe a signal at that time point while resisting the idea that the entire recovery trajectory had clearly improved. 
Agreed, especially because agility and self-rated soreness didn't show consistent advantages. Bing, if a coach mostly needs braking and changes of direction tomorrow, how much weight would you give that better jump when deciding whether this strategy has served its purpose? 
Some weight, but I'd still need information about the movement task the coach actually plans to ask the athlete to perform. 
There's also a local pain finding to keep separate from soreness. The calf pressure pain threshold, meaning pressure at the first sensation of pain, was higher with beetroot juice, but that doesn't establish whole-body pain relief or repaired tissue. 
And the mechanism stays open because nitrate exposure and inflammation weren't directly measured, while the control drink wasn't necessarily inactive. Testing also followed that day's drink, leaving cumulative recovery and an acute effect difficult to separate, even before considering training changes. 
That caution becomes more consequential when pain follows an injury. The hip paper combines one adolescent soccer case with a review of rare iliopsoas avulsions, where the hip flexor attachment can pull away a piece of bone, mostly in adolescent males. 
So a teenager with sudden front-of-hip pain and trouble lifting the leg shouldn't simply be treated as having ordinary soreness? 
Correct, especially with limping or clear weakness after kicking or sprinting, that calls for clinical assessment rather than harder testing. In the reported case, painless functional recovery coexisted with a six-month scan showing incomplete bony union, which requires careful clinical interpretation. 
The literature review included 58 people, with 52 managed conservatively and six surgically, separate from the new case. Those counts can't establish which treatment works better because treatment selection differed, and case reports can't supply an individual clearance rule. 
Right, the clinical question survives the headline. We need similar care with the claim of an ACL epidemic in women's soccer, where this week's perspective article examined historical surveillance and found no clear upward or downward trend in the published data. 
When injuries keep appearing in the news, what comparison should we ask for before deciding the underlying rate has changed? 
Ask about exposure time, league and season, because injury counts alone leave out how much soccer was played. Overall ACL rates across the included studies ranged from 0.09 to 0.24 injuries per thousand hours, which is a range across studies rather than one global estimate. 
And this was a narrative perspective with uneven geographic coverage and missing years, rather than a formal global trend analysis. The absence of a clear increase doesn't make an ACL injury less consequential or tell us prevention and care already have enough resources. 
Care also depends on what people feel able to tell us. The cannabinoid paper used separate anonymous surveys of contact-sport athletes and medical staff, and its use figures came from 105 respondents to that question, with 56 percent reporting current use. 
So the denominator changes by question, and that percentage doesn't describe all 166 recruited athletes or contact-sport athletes generally. 
Exactly, and among 112 people answering the relevant communication questions, only 21.4 percent said they could discuss use comfortably. Bing, what would you change in a recovery conversation while keeping clear that reported benefits don't establish product efficacy or safety? 
I'd ask privately and without judgment about the product, purpose, timing and other medicines, then refer questions to someone with relevant expertise. That's an approach proposed in the report, while this self-selected survey itself tested neither communication effectiveness nor a treatment dose. 
That gives the athlete room to explain what the numbers miss. Bringing everything together, our EDGE SPORT proposal is to record the intended task, the information considered, the adjustment made and what happened afterward, with the athlete involved in reviewing the decision. 
encouraging 
I'd add that this combined workflow hasn't been validated, so keeping records doesn't establish that we can predict injuries or performance. 
Yes, it's a proposal for making judgment reviewable. With an unexplained morning result, we'd check measurement and context, then observe the planned task as appropriate, while new pain, limping or marked weakness would shift the question toward professional assessment. 
And what would change my decision is whether the actual work holds its expected quality, how the athlete responds and what followed comparable sessions before. That's the report's proposed review process, with no universal score or percentage that automatically authorizes more work. 
Then our practical recap is to name the next task, keep feelings and functional outcomes visible separately, and write down why you maintained or changed the plan. Keep clinical decisions with the clinical team, and revisit the result with the athlete rather than defending the original prediction. 
That's a manageable conversation to carry into tomorrow, even when the watch and the person disagree. Read the written weekly report and original sources for the methods, limitations and unresolved reporting issues, and thanks for joining Ying and me on edgeSport4Podcast. 
Only 2 of 43 male soccer workload studies, or 4.6 percent, used dedicated performance tests. 
Common weekly arrangements are descriptive practice patterns rather than established optimal prescriptions. Youth performance evidence is limited and includes inconsistent sample reporting. 
The endurance readiness review reported 14 studies and 418 participants. 
This is not a uniform adult validation sample. An adolescent swimming subgroup conflicts with adult eligibility criteria, tool counts differ within the source and the proposed framework lacks prospective validation. 
Caffeine-free treatments presented as caffeine had a pooled standardized effect of d = 0.49, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.28 to 0.69, across 17 studies and 257 participants compared with baseline. 
The effect is not a percentage improvement or a direct comparison with actual caffeine. Evidence certainty was low, no study had low risk of bias and benefits were not consistent across outcomes. The source opposes deceptive administration in practice. 
Twenty-one female collegiate athletes completed four pre-sleep conditions with three nights per condition, without detected differences in sleep or perceived recovery. 
The trial was not designed to establish equivalence. Short exposure, wearable sleep measurement and the supported collegiate population limit generalization. It did not establish insomnia treatment, long-term benefit or competition effects. 
The beetroot juice trial's main inference used 13 participants completing both periods. The estimated 72-hour countermovement jump advantage was 1.5 centimeters, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.05 to 2.97 centimeters. 
The time-point comparison had Holm-adjusted p = 0.033, while the overall interaction had p = 0.062. This does not establish a changed overall recovery trajectory or justify increased training. 
The estimated 72-hour calf pressure pain threshold advantage was 47.5 mmHg, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 11.80 to 83.28 mmHg. 
This was a local threshold outcome, not whole-body analgesia or tissue repair. Agility and self-rated soreness did not show consistent advantages. Nitrate exposure and inflammatory mechanisms were not verified, the control was potentially active and acute versus accumulated effects could not be fully separated. 
The hip review included 58 literature patients, with 52 managed conservatively and six surgically, separate from the new adolescent case. The new case had incomplete bony union on six-month imaging despite painless functional recovery. 
Case-level evidence is extremely uncertain and cannot establish treatment superiority, a displacement threshold or individual clearance criteria. The written report flags inconsistent injury-side reporting and an unresolved rehabilitation-to-return chronology. 
Across the included women's soccer surveillance studies, overall ACL incidence ranged from 0.09 to 0.24 injuries per 1,000 hours, without a clear upward or downward trend in published data. 
The range is across studies rather than a pooled global estimate. The article is a narrative perspective with geographic and temporal gaps, not a formal global trend test. It does not establish low individual risk or adequate prevention resources. 
Among 105 cannabinoid-use question respondents, 56 percent reported current use. Among 112 respondents to the relevant communication questions, 21.4 percent reported being comfortable discussing use. 
Question-specific denominators must be retained. Self-selected, cross-sectional, self-reported survey findings do not estimate universal prevalence or establish efficacy, safety, dosing or the effectiveness of a communication intervention. 
The proposed EDGE SPORT workflow records the intended task, supporting information, actual adjustment and subsequent response. 
This is an editorial operational proposal rather than a validated combined system. It supplies no universal progression percentage, readiness threshold, injury prediction or medical clearance rule. 
Define the next task before interpreting a readiness score or recovery result. 
Keep subjective comfort, physiological signals and task performance separate. 
Preserve the actual comparison, analysis population and exposure denominator. 
Seek clinical assessment for concerning new symptoms rather than using readiness tests for clearance. 
Record decisions and subsequent responses as an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal. 
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for methods, limitations and unresolved reporting issues.

週課表與準備度分數，足以決定明天加量嗎？ 
男性足球常見的週中高負荷、賽前減量安排已有大量描述，直接驗證表現效益的研究卻只有 2/43 篇；耐力運動的準備度工具也多反映既往疲勞或恢復，尚未充分驗證能預測下一堂訓練。本週結合女性運動員營養試驗、期待效應、傷害監測與溝通資料，提出以主觀感受、生理趨勢及實際任務反應共同決定維持、調整或轉介的流程。 
團隊如何把週課表、晨間監測與恢復策略，轉成可追蹤的下一堂訓練決策？ 
本期完整閱讀所附八篇全文文字：full-text-web 3 篇、full-text-open 5 篇，full-text-local、full-text-excerpt 與 abstract-only 均為 0 篇。全文可核對方法、表格及限制，但補充檔案僅使用附件實際提供的說明與數值；不能因取得全文，就把描述研究、概念框架或小型試驗升級為已驗證的通用處方。 
本週研究地圖 
JSCR 與 IJSPP 的兩篇綜述共同把問題推進到「監測與安排是否真正驗證了下一次表現」；JISSN 三篇研究則分別處理期待效應、睡前進食及甜菜根汁，顯示感受、生理與功能結果需分開解讀。Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine 提供罕見髖部撕脫傷的病例級證據，BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine 校正女足 ACL 趨勢敘事，Sports Health 揭示大麻素使用與照護溝通缺口。這些研究在決策方法上呼應，沒有共同驗證單一準備度分數或加量門檻。

睡前營養交叉試驗的完成樣本與暴露 
NCAA Division I 女性選手；四條件睡眠及恢復結果未檢出顯著差異，並非等效試驗。

女足 ACL 整體發生率的研究間範圍 
頂級聯賽歷史監測資料；地理及時間覆蓋不完整，並非單一全球統合發生率。 
決策前必懂的背景 
先區分做了多少、身體如何反應、目前能否完成指定任務，以及傷後獲准參與到哪個層級。晨間狀態、單次跳躍或症狀改善都能提供資訊，但本週來源未建立可跨運動使用的自動通關規則。 
外在負荷與內在負荷 
外在負荷是實際完成的工作，如時間、距離及加減速；內在負荷是個人對工作的生理與感知反應，如心率及 RPE。 
同樣距離可能引起不同反應；課表與反應應配對保存，並固定速度區間及裝置設定。 
source-stated 
訓練準備度 
準備度綜述提出的操作概念，是個人在當下承受並有效完成下一項身體與認知任務的暫時狀態。 
必須說明準備完成哪項任務，再以隨後訓練品質檢查判斷；作者的多面向框架尚未經前瞻驗證。 
恢復、疲勞與準備度 
恢復與疲勞描述訓練後的狀態或反應；它們與準備度相關，但不能單獨代表下一項任務的能力。 
保留睡眠、痠痛、生理與功能的個別結果，避免合成分數掩蓋不一致。 
cross-source-synthesis 
重返參與、重返運動與重返表現 
依所附 ACL 課程的連續性概念，分別指有限制地參與訓練、恢復運動參與，以及恢復競技表現。 
記錄實際訓練限制與競技層級；一般訓練準備度不能替代傷後醫療回場決策。 
inclass-supported 
壓痛閾值與主觀痠痛 
甜菜根汁研究的壓痛閾值是加壓至首次感到疼痛的壓力；VAS 是選手自評痠痛程度。 
小腿壓痛閾值提高不能改寫為全身止痛，亦不能取代跳躍或變向測試。 
發生率、件數與傷害負擔 
發生率需以暴露時間作分母；每隊每季件數是另一種尺度，而傷害後果不能只用件數概括。 
比較女足 ACL 趨勢時分開訓練、比賽與整體暴露；穩定發生率仍可伴隨重要照護負擔。 
未檢出差異與已證明等效 
沒有顯著差異僅表示該研究未確認條件差，不能自行推成所有方案效果相同。 
睡前營養試驗可提供短期未見不利變化的資訊，不能證明各配方等效或適用所有睡眠狀況。 
期待可能改變感知與表現 
假咖啡因研究以期待與心理生物反應解釋結果，但統合分析不能辨認個人的反應機制，也未分離真咖啡因中的期待占比。 
記錄選手對策略的期待，統一測試說明，採誠實溝通。 
不同任務對恢復的要求不同 
CMJ 是較受限制的爆發任務，排球變向包含煞車、再加速與動作策略；甜菜根汁試驗的兩種結果未同步改善。 
先選擇下一堂課最相關的功能結果，再判斷策略是否有用。 
硝酸鹽機轉尚未被本試驗直接確認 
來源提出硝酸鹽經亞硝酸鹽與一氧化氮路徑可能影響血流及收縮，但試驗未測血中硝酸鹽、亞硝酸鹽或發炎指標，對照亦含其他植物成分。 
不能由跳躍差異宣稱已證實抗發炎、組織修復或硝酸鹽單一成分效果。

sport-medicine 
從追蹤恢復，前進到驗證下一堂課 
相較前期對補充劑量、量測工具與任務特異性的討論，本週新增更直接的方法問題：常見週課表未必已證實最佳，對疲勞敏感的指標也未必能預測未來表現。最可行的整合方向，是保存決策前狀態、實際調整與後續任務品質，逐步檢查團隊自己的判斷；這是一項監測流程提案，並非已驗證的傷害預測模型。 
full-text-open 
系統性回顧與隨機效應統合分析；17 項研究來自 16 份報告，包含交叉與平行設計。

停止運動並緊急轉介，優先排除危及肢體的神經血管傷害。 
由處理急症的醫療團隊確認後續照護與活動條件。 
urgent-referral 
新增產品後不適，或大麻素／合併藥物暴露資訊不足 
暫停新增策略的進階評估，轉介具相關能力的醫療或營養人員；不由問卷結果自行訂劑量。 
用途、暴露、風險與監測責任已釐清，並有專業評估。 
決策品質 
課前判斷、調整理由與當堂結果 
每次關鍵課後，微週期回顧 
檢查判斷與任務完成是否一致，不宣稱已達預測效度。 
功能

依課程需求及可耐受頻率

睡眠與感受 
固定題目的睡眠、疲勞、痠痛與壓力 
晨間及症狀改變時 
保留單項變化，不能以舒服推定全面恢復。 
暴露與耐受 
實際訓練量、產品使用與不適紀錄 
每堂及新增策略期間 
分辨實際執行、期待與功能反應；未建立的安全界線不自行補值。

臨床症狀、活動限制及實際參與層級

本流程未被證明能降低傷害；晨間資料正常或跳得較高均不代表沒有傷害風險。 
男性足球、成人耐力、女性大學營養試驗及青少年髖傷資料不能直接互換處方。 
睡眠未檢出不利變化不等於所有睡前食品、劑量及睡眠障礙族群均安全適用。 
女足 ACL 監測未見明確上升，仍需預防、資源與適當照護，避免以恐嚇或淡化方式溝通。 
大麻素自陳受益不是療效證明；保密詢問有助完整評估，但本文未驗證任何教育或用藥流程。 
哪些準備度組合可可靠預測下一堂課的品質及耐受，仍待前瞻驗證。 
最佳週負荷峰值日、賽前時長與先發／替補補償劑量未確立。 
本週未建立通用基線天數、進退階分數、加量百分比或恢復期限。 
營養試驗的長期效果、實際競賽轉移及不同女性族群反應仍不清楚。 
髂腰肌大位移撕脫的長期功能、未癒合後果與手術比較仍缺可靠資料。

Feeling Better, Ready for What? 
Recovery, nutrition, strength and the next task 
Ying and Bing explore eight sources on cold water, elastic bands, protein, recreational sports nutrition, weight reduction, creatine, ACL return outcomes and injection safety. They ask when an improved measurement actually supports the next task, while keeping study findings, clinical decisions and editorial proposals distinct.

Distinguish feeling recovered from performance on a specific task at a specific time. 
Separate acute protein synthesis, daily nutrition needs and weight reduction guidance. 
Explain why analysis populations, outcome definitions and denominators change interpretation. 
Recognize the limits of laboratory safety signals and observational return-to-sport associations. 
Describe an explicitly unvalidated approach to reviewing a strategy with the athlete. 
Brand pronunciation: edgeSport4Podcast is spoken as Edge Sport for Podcast. 
All research discussion comes from the supplied 2026-w43 weekly report. No relatedIssues research is used. 
Cold water: a 15-person crossover trial compared two combined temperature and duration protocols with seated rest. 
Elastic bands: the female soccer trial found selected strength signals without clear additional jump or change-of-direction benefits. 
Protein synthesis: the network meta-analysis measured responses over hours, rather than long-term muscle growth. 
Sports nutrition: the ten-expert session is a narrative meeting summary. Its marathon carbohydrate figures are model estimates. 
Weight reduction: the ISSN position statement combines evidence from different populations and does not supply universal athlete targets. 
Creatine: the breath-hold cycling performance signal depended on the analysis population and did not establish underwater benefit or safety-based progression criteria for underwater training based on this trial's findings and limitations as reported in the weekly report. 
Feeling better before the next task 
Cold water illustrates why timing and the selected performance test matter. 
When strength does and doesn't transfer 
Elastic band training improves selected measures without establishing broader performance or injury benefits. 
Protein over hours and nutrition over days 
Acute synthesis rankings, recreational fueling and weight reduction answer different questions. 
A result that changes with the analysis 
The creatine breath-hold trial offers a tentative laboratory signal. 
What counts as returning? 
ACL outcomes depend on sport, level and available denominators. 
Pain relief, tissue safety and a reviewable decision 
Injection evidence requires careful denominators, followed by a practical editorial proposal. 
You've finished training and someone asks whether you feel ready to go again. I'd want to ask what we're doing next. Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and this week's question is when feeling better actually supports the next task.

I'm Bing. That question gets awkward when the athlete feels better but the test looks worse. We've got eight sources today that make us separate comfort, strength, nutrition signals and actual participation. What would make us change the plan rather than just admire a number? 
curious 
Cold water gives us a concrete example. Fifteen male university soccer players completed all three conditions after bodyweight squats to exhaustion. Each player tried water at fifteen degrees Celsius for eleven minutes, ten degrees for two and a half minutes, and seated rest. 
clear 
So this compares two packages of temperature and time. It doesn't tell us what colder water alone would do. 
reflective 
Exactly, and their immediate tests happened at different elapsed times. After the longer immersion, the average twenty metre sprint took 3.47 seconds. After the shorter immersion it took 3.26 seconds, with a statistically significant difference between those two conditions. 
Lower is faster, so the shorter package looked better there. Rest averaged 3.32 seconds, but that doesn't establish every possible pairwise difference. What happened when they jumped rather than sprinted? That's where I'd worry about calling someone generally recovered. 
The countermovement jump, a downward movement followed by a vertical jump, was lower immediately after the longer immersion than after either alternative. Average heights were about thirty five centimetres after the longer immersion, thirty eight after the shorter one and thirty nine after rest. 
That makes the next task matter. Did the picture change when the players had a day to recover? 
At twenty four hours, both cold water conditions had faster sprints than rest. That doesn't establish that the longer protocol was better than the shorter one the next day, and the study didn't show a consistent soreness or intermittent endurance advantage. 
cautious 
I'd keep that fairly narrow. These were young men with cold water experience, using a squat fatigue model rather than a match. Reduced fatigue feelings alongside poorer immediate jumping are useful evidence against letting one reassuring answer settle the whole decision. 
The same question comes up with training. If a team gets stronger, what else has improved? The female soccer trial added supervised elastic band work twice a week for nine weeks to normal training and matches across three age groups. 
There were seventy four players after the intervention and sixty six at follow-up. The clearest strength signal was in the under nineteen group, but extra training time wasn't matched in the control group. I'd hesitate before attributing everything specifically to the bands. 
Would that hesitation stop you trying it with a similar team that has limited access to equipment? 
It wouldn't automatically stop a supervised trial. I'd explain that selected knee strength measures improved, while jumps and change of direction showed no clear additional benefit. If the coach wants faster cutting, we'd still need to measure that rather than substitute a strength result. 
And we couldn't sell it as injury prevention. The trial didn't measure injury reduction, and strength estimates falling after three weeks without the bands weren't statistically significant changes. That leaves uncertainty about maintenance, rather than proof that everyone quickly loses the gains. 
Useful equipment, potentially useful strength changes, and still a separate question about football performance. I can work with that. 
That separation gets harder when a supplement comes with a ranking. Our protein review combined fifty one studies of single protein sources after resistance exercise. Its main outcome was muscle protein synthesis, meaning the rate of making new muscle protein over the measured hours. 
Measured with amino acid tracers and muscle biopsies, rather than watching muscle size change over months. In the primary network analysis, only whey had a statistically significant advantage over control. How large was that difference in the actual unit? 
The mean difference was 0.02 percentage points per hour, with a confidence interval from 0.01 to 0.04. It's an acute synthesis measurement, so we can't multiply it through the calendar and promise a particular amount of extra muscle. 
What about a source near the top of the ranking? Wouldn't that still be our best bet? 
Only with considerable caution. Native whey and pea protein had sparse evidence, with just one and two study arms respectively. The network also had substantial heterogeneity and inconsistency, so rank alone is a shaky reason to change someone's shopping or claim equivalence. 
Then I'd ask about the daily diet before choosing a winner. The ten-expert sports nutrition session helps with that broader question, though it's a narrative meeting summary. It isn't a new trial or a systematic comparison of every recommendation. 
It also challenges the idea that all nutrition guidance comes from elite athletes. The summary cites an audit in which only eighty one of eighteen hundred and sixty seven supplement studies included the highest athlete tiers, about four percent. That's a cited audit, not new recruitment here. 
So being recreational doesn't make guidance irrelevant. Which details would you need before translating it to an actual session? 
Duration, intensity, total intake and tolerance. Its marathon model estimated lower carbohydrate per hour for a four hour runner than a two hour runner, yet a higher total over the race. Those were model estimates, but they show why hourly and total amounts answer different questions. 
And a practical protein target isn't a minimum admission ticket for exercise benefits. The session treats 1.6 grams per kilogram per day as useful for many people, rather than a line below which training stops helping. Does weight reduction change the context again? 
Yes. The weight reduction position statement distinguishes general adults, people doing resistance training, and lean resistance-trained adults in an energy deficit. Its higher protein ranges for that last situation are contextual recommendations, rather than competing answers to the same experiment. 
I'd be more interested in preserving function than winning a weekly weigh-in. Does the statement support that priority? 
It puts adequate protein, resistance training and a sustainable energy deficit together. Much of the longer-term evidence comes from overweight or obese adults, so applying it to very lean athletes needs care, and it doesn't cover adolescent weight reduction or acute dehydration cuts. 
That also changes how I'd read a plateau. The statement doesn't let us diagnose metabolic damage from stable weight, and short-term fat-free mass changes can include water and glycogen. If strength or training quality keeps falling, I'd reopen the plan rather than deepen restriction automatically. 
Water also complicates the creatine study, where short-term fat-free mass changes can't simply be called new muscle. Twenty trained breath-hold divers were randomized to creatine or placebo for seven days, then tested during breath-hold cycling in a laboratory. 
And this one makes the analysis population unusually important. What changed when everyone randomized was kept in the analysis? 
The analysis excluding one creatine participant found significant differences in changes in cycling distance and breath-hold duration. The intention-to-treat analysis, which retained all twenty randomized participants, didn't confirm those performance differences, with interaction p values of 0.121 and 0.093. 
That doesn't prove there was no effect, but it makes the apparent benefit less robust. With a small sample, baseline differences and possible learning effects, I'd describe a finding worth checking rather than a reliable performance gain. Did any other signal remain? 
The lactate accumulation difference remained significant in the intention-to-treat analysis. But lower peripheral lactate doesn't establish delayed acidosis or safer oxygen deprivation, and the device distance reported in metres isn't a measurement of mechanical work in joules. 
So nothing here supports extending a maximal breath hold or assuming less underwater risk. They didn't test post-supplement underwater performance at all. That's a clear example of a laboratory result that can't carry the practical conclusion someone might most want from it. 
Return after ACL reconstruction has its own version of that gap. This secondary analysis involved five hundred young people who had played cutting, jumping or pivoting sports. What would you want a study to mean when it says they returned? 
I'd want to know whether they resumed any sport, a high-risk sport, or their original sport at their old level. Within two years, four hundred and thirty of four hundred and ninety seven returned to any sport, about eighty seven percent. 
But original sport and level was two hundred and twenty five of four hundred and ninety four, about forty six percent. Different available denominators, and a substantially different outcome. Returning to high-risk sport at any level sat between them, at three hundred and eighty of four hundred and ninety seven. 
That makes the word returned feel incomplete. How should we explain the sex difference without overstating it? 
Women had lower adjusted odds of returning to high-risk sport, with an odds ratio of 0.47 in the sensitivity model. Odds compare returning with not returning, so that isn't a statement that women's probability was forty seven percent of men's. 
And sex wasn't randomized, even though the parent study randomized surgery. These associations can't establish individual clearance rules or prove that changing confidence causes return, and choosing a lower-risk activity needn't be treated as failure if it fits the person's goals. 
That respect for the person's goals belongs in treatment conversations too. The local anaesthetic review mapped thirty nine sources on musculoskeletal injections, mixing clinical descriptions with laboratory evidence. All twelve experimental studies were outside the body, and there was no formal risk-of-bias assessment. 
Its striking number is twenty nine of thirty nine sources mentioning cell toxicity. That denominator is papers, not injected patients, so seventy four point three percent isn't a patient's chance of harm. What concern can we responsibly carry into a clinical discussion? 
The review repeatedly raises concentration, exposure time and continuous infusion into a joint, particularly around cartilage toxicity. Those patterns warrant discussion, but they don't establish a safe concentration or a fixed harm rate for a single injection, and pain relief can't establish tissue safety. 
I'd ask the treating clinician what the anaesthetic is intended to achieve, what alternatives exist and how it'll be given. That keeps the concern useful without turning a mixed evidence map into instructions for choosing a drug or changing its dose ourselves. 
Across these examples, I want a modest decision record. Write down the task, the timing, what changed and what would make us reconsider. That's our EDGE SPORT proposal for organizing a discussion, and these eight sources haven't jointly validated it. 
I'd add the athlete's experience beside the functional result. Keep the comparison as consistent as practical and look for a benefit we can reproduce without an unacceptable cost. That remains our editorial approach, with no universal improvement threshold or permission to bypass medical assessment. 
And I'd leave room for the goal to change. Someone may value comfort, another person may need jumping performance, and someone returning after surgery may choose a different sport. We can ask what matters without pretending those are the same outcome. 
That's a useful conversation to take into the next session. Name the task before judging the strategy, and keep the limits beside the result. For the full methods, numbers and unresolved reporting issues, visit the written weekly report and its original sources. Thanks for joining us. 
Fifteen male university soccer players completed a crossover comparison of 15°C for 11 minutes, 10°C for 2.5 minutes and seated rest. Immediate mean sprint times were 3.47, 3.26 and 3.32 seconds respectively. 
The two immersion protocols differed significantly from each other. Temperature and duration changed together, and immediate tests occurred at different elapsed times. The values do not establish that every pairwise comparison was significant. 
Immediate mean countermovement jump heights were 34.67, 37.67 and 38.76 centimetres for longer immersion, shorter immersion and rest. The longer immersion was lower than both alternatives. Both immersion conditions produced faster sprints than rest at 24 hours. 
Dialogue rounds jump heights for listening. The trial did not establish longer immersion superiority the next day or consistent soreness and intermittent endurance benefits. 
The female soccer trial added elastic band training twice weekly for nine weeks. There were 74 participants after intervention and 66 at follow-up, with selected strength signals but no clear additional jump or change-of-direction benefits. 
The control did not match additional training time or attention. Injury prevention was not measured, and detraining-period changes were not statistically significant. The packet flags inconsistencies between abstract and body strength statistics. 
The protein network meta-analysis included 51 studies. In its primary model, whey versus control increased acute muscle protein synthesis by 0.02 percentage points per hour, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.01 to 0.04. 
This concerns responses over hours after exercise. It does not establish long-term hypertrophy, optimal doses or plant versus animal equivalence. Native whey and pea estimates came from only one and two study arms, with substantial network heterogeneity and inconsistency. 
The ten-expert session cites an audit in which 81 of 1867 supplement studies, about 4%, included Tier 4–5 athletes. It presents 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram per day as a practical target for many people rather than a necessary threshold for exercise benefit. 
This is a narrative expert-session summary. The audit is cited background rather than a new analysis. Marathon carbohydrate comparisons are model estimates rather than tested prescriptions. 
The weight reduction position statement combines sustainable energy restriction, sufficient protein and resistance training, with recommendations that vary by population and energy context. 
It is a qualitative position statement without formal GRADE assessment. Much long-term evidence comes from overweight or obese adults. It does not cover adolescent weight reduction or acute dehydration cuts, and stable weight alone cannot diagnose metabolic damage. 
The creatine trial randomized 20 trained breath-hold divers for seven days. The 19-person per-protocol analysis found significant distance and duration interactions, while the 20-person intention-to-treat analysis yielded p=0.121 and p=0.093 respectively. 
Non-significance does not prove absence of effect. Results were sensitive to analysis population, and the report flags internal exclusion-count inconsistencies. The task was laboratory cycling, not post-supplement underwater performance. 
The creatine trial retained a lactate accumulation interaction in intention-to-treat analysis, p=0.001. 
Peripheral lactate cannot establish delayed acidosis or improved hypoxia safety. Device distance in metres is not mechanical work in joules, and short-term fat-free mass change is not established muscle growth. 
Within two years after ACL reconstruction, return to any sport was 430/497, 86.5%; return to high-risk sport was 380/497, 76.5%; and return to original high-risk sport and level was 225/494, 45.5%. 
Dialogue rounds the any-sport and original-level percentages. Outcomes have different available denominators. This is a selected young high-risk population, excluding graft ruptures before six months, rather than all reconstruction patients. 
Women had lower adjusted odds of returning to high-risk sport in a sensitivity model, OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.29–0.76, model n=454. 
An odds ratio is not a probability ratio. Sex associations are observational despite the randomized surgical parent trial. These models do not establish causal confidence interventions or individual clearance criteria. 
The injection scoping review included 39 sources, with 29/39, 74.3%, mentioning cell toxicity. All 12 experimental studies were in vitro. 
The percentage describes sources, not patient incidence. Evidence categories may overlap. No formal risk-of-bias assessment was conducted, and the review does not establish absolute clinical risk or safe concentrations. 
Recording the task, timing, comparison, response and reasons to reconsider is an EDGE SPORT editorial proposal. 
The integrated workflow was not jointly validated by these studies. It supplies no universal change threshold, treatment prescription or medical clearance rule. 
Define the next task and its timing before interpreting an improvement. 
Keep comfort, strength, acute synthesis, tissue safety and actual participation distinct. 
Check the analysis population, denominator and uncertainty beside every headline number. 
Review repeatable benefits and costs with the athlete. This integrated EDGE SPORT approach remains unvalidated.

冷水後衝刺恢復、跳躍仍下降：恢復策略如何對準下一項任務？ 
本週八篇來源把恢復、營養、肌力與回場的共同問題具體化：改善一項指標，能否支持下一項任務？冷水浸泡的效益隨時間與測試改變，彈力帶肌力增益未同步轉成跳躍或變向優勢；蛋白質、減重與肌酸資料也要求區分急性反應、長期適應與分析穩健性。實務上應先定義目標、核對族群及量測，再用功能、耐受與健康反應決定保留或調整策略。 
團隊如何依下一項任務與恢復時間，選擇並驗證營養、恢復或訓練策略，而不把單項改善當成全面準備完成？ 
本期共八篇：full-text-web 2 篇、full-text-open 6 篇，full-text-local、full-text-excerpt、abstract-only 各 0 篇；依提供的完整嵌入全文、表格、圖說及可見補充說明整理。完整文字提高設計與結果查核能力，但未提供實際內容的補充檔仍不能視為已核實；專家會議摘要、立場聲明、範疇回顧及試驗的證據用途須分開。 
本週研究地圖 
JSCR 的冷水交叉試驗新增急性與延遲恢復的直接比較；JISSN 同時涵蓋蛋白質網絡統合、肌酸憋氣試驗與減重立場聲明。Sports Health 的女足試驗及 ACL 次級分析提醒，力量、運動參與與原有競技層級是不同結果；IJSNEM 與 BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine 則分別補上營養外推與注射風險的邊界。各篇共同支持情境化判讀，未共同驗證一套通用準備度門檻。

年輕高風險族群 ACL 重建後兩年內；三種結果定義與可用分母不同。

提到細胞毒性的來源 
局部麻醉範疇回顧的文獻分布，並非注射患者的不良事件機率。 
決策前必懂的背景 
恢復感、測試表現、組織安全與實際運動參與需分別量測。本週資料支持先選定決策結果，再檢查時間、比較條件及分析族群；沒有單一生理指標可以涵蓋全部準備度。 
急性肌肉蛋白質合成率（MPS／FSR） 
以示蹤胺基酸與肌肉切片估計，短時間內新合成肌肉蛋白的比例。 
本期網絡統合主要涵蓋運動後數小時，不能把每小時差異累加推算長期肌肉增加。 
source-stated 
瘦軟組織與去脂體重（FFM） 
瘦軟組織不含骨礦物；FFM 包含全部非脂肪組織。 
短期變化可能包含水分與肝醣，肌酸後 FFM 上升不能直接稱為增肌。 
限制性參與、重返運動與重返表現 
課程的參與階段容許受限訓練，後續才是完整專項與競技表現；本期 ACL 研究另以任何運動、高風險運動及原有高風險運動層級分類。 
紀錄時同時寫出限制、運動種類與層級；研究的 RTA 不能直接等同臨床分期中的限制性參與。 
cross-source-synthesis 
勝算比（OR） 
比較結果發生與未發生之勝算的相對數值。 
OR 0.47 表示調整後勝算較低，不能寫成女性回場機率只有男性的 47%。 
依方案分析與意向治療分析（ITT） 
前者依遵循方案條件選取分析樣本，後者保留全部隨機分派者。 
兩者結論不同時，應揭露排除個案對效果穩健性的影響。 
保留次數（RIR） 
完成一組後，自評仍能完成的重複次數。 
女足研究以約 2RIR 調整彈力阻力；這是該方案的負荷工具，非回場門檻。 
降溫可能同時改變感受與神經肌肉輸出 
冷水試驗觀察到疲勞感下降與立即跳躍下降並存；神經傳導、肌溫與自主神經的解釋並未由直接機轉量測確認。 
接受恢復處置後仍須檢查下一項任務，不宜只問是否比較舒服。 
蛋白質支持適應，但結果仍取決於訓練與能量情境 
急性合成訊號、持續能量不足下的蛋白平衡與長期肌肉保留屬不同尺度；減重聲明將足量蛋白質與阻力訓練並列。 
先確認每日攝取、訓練刺激及能量限制，再討論來源或單次時機。 
局部止痛與組織風險並存 
局部麻醉藉鈉離子通道阻斷降低神經傳導；細胞實驗與臨床描述則提示濃度、暴露時間及給藥方式可能影響毒性。 
止痛後的感受不能取代醫療評估，風險亦不能由體外結果直接量化。

從「有改善」走向「改善哪項任務、何時成立」 
本週進展在於拆開常被合併的結果：較少疲勞感未必伴隨立即跳躍恢復，膝肌力增加未必改善變向，急性 MPS 排名未必預測增肌，回到任何運動也未必回到原有層級。這延續前期功能驗證方向，並新增分析樣本、結果定義與時間點會改變判斷的具體案例。

日本季中 15 名健康男性大學足球員，18–19 歲，皆有冷水經驗並完成全部測量。

Better Numbers, Better Decisions? 
Supplements, useful measurements, and the distance between improvement and readiness. 
Ying and Bing discuss caffeine in male boxers, tangeretin in female combat athletes, cinnamon and functional training in military cadets, a Canadian dietary questionnaire, and concussion surveillance in community rugby. They ask what would justify keeping a strategy while separating measured changes from competition benefits and medical clearance. 
en

cohost

Analytical partner · male voice
