Distinguish laboratory improvements, body changes, and absence records from competition benefits and clearance. 
Explain why improvement within one group does not establish superiority over a comparator. 
Interpret supplement findings with their populations, task comparisons, measurement limits, and reporting inconsistencies. 
Distinguish questionnaire relevance and comprehension from accuracy and reliability. 
Describe an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT approach to reviewing a new strategy. 
The supplied weeklyReport is the sole source for research claims. No additional research or historical evidence is introduced. 
Caffeine in male boxers: https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2743368 
Tangeretin in female combat athletes: https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2740800 
Functional training and cinnamon in military cadets: https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2743157 
Canadian adaptation of the Athlete Diet Index: https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2741897 
Community rugby concussion surveillance: https://doi.org/10.1177/19417381261474860 
Research doses and follow-up periods describe study exposures. They are not listener prescriptions. 
The weekly report flags inconsistencies in the tangeretin, cinnamon, and rugby papers. Interpretations remain conservative pending editorial verification. 
What would make a change worth keeping? 
A better number needs a clearly defined task and comparison. 
Caffeine and the task being tested 
Dose comparisons in boxers support selected laboratory outcomes without establishing punching benefits. 
Weight change and functional benefit 
Tangeretin findings illustrate the difference between body composition signals and intervention-specific performance gains. 
Training, cinnamon, and uncertain attribution 
Military fitness changes deserve attention alongside design and reporting limitations. 
A questionnaire people can understand 
Canadian dietary tool adaptation supports relevance and comprehension while leaving other measurement properties unverified. 
Absence, recovery, and the next decision 
Rugby surveillance describes care burden without supplying personal clearance dates. The conversation closes with an explicitly unvalidated review proposal. 
Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and I can imagine the relief of seeing a better test result after trying something new. This week's question is what that improvement actually gives us permission to change. 
warm 
And I'm Bing. We say edgeSport4Podcast as Edge Sport for Podcast. Over coffee I'd probably ask the awkward follow-up. Did the athlete get better at the thing they care about, or did one number get better? 
curious 
That's the thread through all five papers. We've got three supplement studies, a dietary questionnaire, and rugby concussion records. They measure very different things, so we need to decide what each result can reasonably support before we act. 
clear 
Could we start with the athlete's question before opening the spreadsheet? What change would actually make their training or competition better? 
Yes, and the boxer study makes that concrete. Fifteen trained male boxers each completed placebo, three milligrams of caffeine per kilogram, and six milligrams per kilogram. The randomized crossover design let researchers compare conditions in the same people. 
That comparison is useful because we're less dependent on differences between athletes. But were they punching, or testing capacities that might matter for punching? I'd want that distinction settled before calling the result a boxing benefit. 
They tested jumping, explosive push-off performance, and joint torque at fixed movement speeds. They didn't measure punches or competition. In the later testing block, the lower caffeine dose increased countermovement jump height by 0.039 meters compared with placebo. 
So that's 3.9 centimeters on a jump test. What happened with the higher dose, and was its advantage actually established? 
The higher dose was 0.051 meters above placebo. The confidence intervals were 0.019 to 0.059 meters for the lower dose and 0.032 to 0.071 for the higher dose. They didn't detect a significant difference between doses. 
Then the larger average doesn't establish that more is better for jumping. It also doesn't establish the doses are equivalent. Did any task give a clearer direct comparison between the two caffeine doses? 
reflective 
Knee extension torque did. In that later block, the higher dose exceeded placebo by 41.36 newton meters and the lower dose by 25.98 newton meters. That's a specific finding at the tested movement speed, rather than a general dose advantage. 
Specific is doing a lot of work there. What about the explosive push-off test, where measurement noise could change the interpretation? 
Higher-dose average power exceeded placebo by 137.3 watts, but baseline typical error was 104.20 watts. That error describes repeat measurement fluctuation. The direct dose comparison wasn't significant, and one exposure per dose couldn't establish a stable individual response. 
cautious 
I'd want repeated task benefits and tolerability before keeping it. The later block began around sixty minutes, but tests continued afterward. We can't call that everyone's precise peak, especially when caffeine concentration wasn't measured and side effects were only asked about verbally. 
That same need to name the benefit carries into weight management. What would persuade you that a supplement helped a combat athlete? A lower scale reading, making a weight category, or preserving the ability to train and compete? 
I'd want those questions kept separate. Making weight matters to eligibility, but it doesn't by itself tell me how the athlete performs or feels. 
The tangeretin trial enrolled thirty female combat athletes, fifteen per group. For thirty days, one group received four hundred milligrams daily alongside whey protein, while the comparator received whey. This happened during winter training with centralized meals and normal drinking. 
So it wasn't a rapid dehydration experiment. The supplemented group's mean weight went from 61.58 to 60.86 kilograms, while the comparator went from 60.96 to 61.26. Was there evidence that those patterns differed beyond a descriptive contrast? 
Yes, the group by time interaction for weight was significant. That asks whether the groups changed differently over time. Body fat percentage also showed an interaction, with the supplemented group's mean falling from 23.92 to 22.92 percent. 
That's about one percentage point in body fat. Do the individual weight-loss counts tell us anything beyond those average changes? 
Twelve of fifteen supplemented athletes lost weight, compared with six of fifteen controls. Those are descriptive counts without a reported statistical comparison of the proportions. And the report flags body composition totals that don't clearly reconcile with body weight. 
That makes me cautious about treating the body composition table as a settled explanation. There's also a performance trap here. If aerobic capacity improves significantly in one group but not the other, have we proved the supplement helped? 
No, we still need the comparison between changes. The aerobic capacity interaction had a p value of 0.445, and time to exhaustion had 0.166. Neither established an intervention-specific improvement, despite favorable changes within the supplemented group. 
Then there's a preliminary body change signal, with reporting questions, rather than demonstrated competition benefit. Thirty days in a small mixed-sport sample also leaves long-term safety unresolved. Weight loss can't clear concerns about low energy availability or justify rapid weight cutting. 
Agreed. Now suppose someone says the military study is stronger because it measured a functional fitness test. Would that make you more willing to consider the cinnamon addition, or would you still start with how the groups were compared? 
I'd welcome a functional outcome, then inspect the comparison. What did the training group do, and what did cinnamon add to it? 
The four groups received Tabata-style functional training, cinnamon, both, or usual military activity. Forty-eight male cadets were randomized and forty-five completed the six weeks. The cinnamon exposure was 1.5 grams daily, and supplementation had no placebo. 
The combined group's Army Combat Fitness Test score rose from 443.6 to 497.2 points, among thirteen completers. That's a visible change, but a before-and-after increase doesn't isolate cinnamon. What happened against training alone? 
The thirteen training-only completers went from 429.6 to 466.8 points. The paper reports the combined group outperforming training alone after accounting for baseline. That deserves attention, although starting scores differed and the analysis included only people who finished. 
So we shouldn't erase the positive comparison. But without a supplement placebo, and with inconsistent reporting, confidence in the extra benefit is limited. 
Exactly. Three sessions weekly over six weeks conflicts with a reported twenty-four sessions. The lean mass increase is also described inconsistently. How would you handle the reported rise in irisin, a blood marker discussed as a possible link to adaptation? 
As something that changed alongside function, without proof it caused the improvement. I'd want clearer reporting and a stronger replication before routine cinnamon use. Even the six fitness components weren't uniformly superior, since the leg tuck comparison wasn't significant. 
That caution about what a measure establishes also applies to the Canadian Athlete Diet Index. Researchers adapted an Australian tool through expert review, English and French translation, and athlete testing. The question here was whether its content and language fit. 
Fit is useful. But if athletes understand the questions, have we learned whether their answers accurately describe what they're eating? 
Not from this study. Of forty-nine athletes, forty-four found it relevant or very relevant and thirty-nine found it easy or very easy to understand. Those results support acceptability and comprehension, rather than accuracy against a dietary reference measure. 
And the final tool has ninety-eight questions, with thirty-six scored and sixty-two unscored. That suggests the surrounding context deserves attention too. Would you explain the kinds of validity they supported, without making them sound interchangeable? 
Face validity asks whether a tool seems understandable and sensible to users. Content validity asks whether it covers the intended material. The Canadian adaptation supports those, while accuracy against a suitable reference and reliability still need study. 
Then I'd use its adaptation process as a useful example when checking local foods, language, and training circumstances. I'd avoid borrowing its score as a Taiwan diagnostic threshold. The sample covered only triathlon, hockey, and athletics, so broader fit also remains open. 
That leaves the rugby study, where the measured outcome was absence after concussion. Across six seasons of Irish community rugby, researchers recorded 456 events in 369 players. The surveillance covered 5,740 player-seasons, which includes repeated seasonal participation rather than that many unique people. 
So both players and events matter to the denominator. What did the absence records show, and how much was shaped by policy? 
Absence data were available for 454 of 456 events. Men's median absence was twenty-four days and women's was twenty-eight. The middle half ranged from twenty-one to thirty-three days for men and twenty-one to forty-two for women. 
And the local adult policy required at least twenty-one days before return. Those distributions therefore include a policy floor. We can't read the medians as pure biological recovery times, or book an individual athlete's return from them. 
Right. Nor did the study measure return to previous performance. More recorded match events occurred in the second half, but that doesn't prove fatigue caused them. Would you treat that pattern as a reason to change prevention training? 
I'd keep recognition and reporting attentive throughout play, but this study didn't test a prevention program. Position counts weren't adjusted for exposure either. The longer female absences are a care burden signal, without identifying one biological cause or an individual's recovery date. 
That's a useful place to bring the week together. A higher jump, a lighter body, a fitness score, an understandable questionnaire, and fewer absent days each answer a different question. None supplies a universal permission slip for competition or the next intervention. 
Our EDGE SPORT proposal is to write down the target task and comparison before trying a change. Then review repeatable task results alongside diet, discomfort, sleep, and recovery. That combined workflow hasn't been validated by these studies, and it provides no universal cutoff. 
encouraging 
And write down what would change your mind. We'd reconsider when benefits don't repeat, conditions can't be compared, or health costs emerge. Suspected concussion needs professional assessment, while participation, competition, and previous performance deserve separate records. That's our operational proposal, not individual medical clearance. 
I like leaving room to revise the decision without blaming the athlete for an uncertain result. Pick the question, check the comparison, and keep the person's experience beside the numbers. The written weekly report and original sources have the methods and unresolved reporting details. 
Fifteen male boxers completed placebo, 3 mg/kg caffeine, and 6 mg/kg caffeine in a randomized double-blind crossover trial. 
Small male-only sample. Each dose was tested once. Research exposures do not establish a preferred competition dose or stable individual response. 
In the later testing block, jump height differences versus placebo were 0.039 m for 3 mg/kg, with 95% CI 0.019–0.059, and 0.051 m for 6 mg/kg, with 95% CI 0.032–0.071. 
The doses did not differ significantly for this outcome. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalence. The block began at 60 minutes and tests extended approximately to 75 minutes. Punching and competition were not measured. 
Higher-dose caffeine increased knee extension peak torque by 41.36 N·m versus placebo and 25.98 N·m versus lower-dose caffeine. 
This was a task-specific result in the later block at a tested speed of 60 degrees per second. It does not establish a general higher-dose advantage. 
Higher-dose caffeine increased explosive push-off mean power by 137.3 W versus placebo. Baseline typical error was 104.20 W. 
The direct dose comparison was not significant. Typical error informs repeat measurement variability and is not a universal benefit threshold. Adverse effects were collected only through verbal questioning. 
Thirty female combat athletes were randomized into two groups of fifteen for 30 days of tangeretin plus whey versus whey alone. The tangeretin exposure was 400 mg daily. 
The study used centralized meals and normal drinking during winter training. It did not test rapid dehydration, different tangeretin doses, actual competition, or long-term safety. 
Mean weight changed from 61.58 to 60.86 kg with tangeretin and from 60.96 to 61.26 kg in controls. The weight interaction p value was 0.018. Supplemented-group body fat changed from 23.92% to 22.92%, with interaction p = 0.008. 
The body fat change is approximately one percentage point. Reported body composition totals and definitions require verification. These changes do not establish competition benefit or absence of low energy availability. 
Weight loss occurred in 12/15 supplemented athletes and 6/15 controls. Aerobic capacity and time-to-exhaustion interaction p values were 0.445 and 0.166. 
The individual weight-loss counts were descriptive without a reported between-group proportion test. Aerobic results did not establish intervention-specific improvements. Significant change within one group alone does not demonstrate superiority. 
The military cadet trial randomized 48 men and analyzed 45 completers across training, cinnamon, combined, and usual-activity groups over six weeks. Cinnamon exposure was 1.5 g daily. 
Supplementation lacked a placebo. Completer-only analysis, baseline differences, and reporting inconsistencies limit attribution and generalizability. 
Combined-group fitness scores increased from 443.6 to 497.2 points and training-only scores from 429.6 to 466.8 points, with thirteen completers in each group. The paper reports a baseline-adjusted combined-group advantage. 
Raw within-group increases do not isolate cinnamon's effect. The reported combined-versus-training comparison deserves conservative consideration. Leg tuck did not show a significant between-group result, with p = 0.152. 
The military paper reports three weekly sessions over six weeks but also twenty-four sessions, and describes lean mass changes inconsistently. 
Training dose should not be copied before verification. BIA hydration control was limited. Concurrent irisin and functional changes do not establish mediation, synergy, or injury prevention. 
The final Canadian Athlete Diet Index has 98 questions, including 36 scored and 62 unscored. In athlete testing, 44/49 found it relevant and 39/49 found it easy to understand. 
These findings support content and face validity, comprehension, and acceptability. Canadian construct validity, criterion validity, and reliability remain to be studied. Australian validation cannot be transferred automatically. 
The dietary tool trial sample represented triathlon, hockey, and athletics. 
The convenience sample does not establish universal sport applicability, a Taiwan version, diagnostic thresholds, or RED-S diagnosis. 
Define the task and comparison before interpreting an improvement. 
Keep weight, laboratory capacity, biomarkers, and competition outcomes distinct. 
Check reporting consistency and measurement suitability before adopting a strategy. 
Treat concussion absence records as group context. They do not supply individual clearance dates or demonstrate restored performance. 
Recording repeatable benefits, tolerability, and reasons to revise a decision is an unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal. 
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for methods, limitations, and unresolved discrepancies.

補充品有效就能上場？拳擊劑量、減重與功能驗證 
本週三項介入研究提示，咖啡因、橘皮素及肉桂搭配訓練的效果，必須依任務、比較條件與量測品質分別判讀；實驗室輸出、體重下降或生物標記改變，都不能直接代表競賽受益。加拿大飲食工具調適與社區橄欖球腦震盪追蹤進一步提醒，評估工具的適用性與傷後缺席紀錄，也是決定是否改變策略的重要邊界。 
團隊如何判斷新增補充品或訓練策略值得保留，同時避免把體重、實驗室數值或缺席天數當成競賽效益與上場許可？ 
本期共五篇：full-text-open 5 篇；full-text-web、full-text-local、full-text-excerpt、abstract-only 各 0 篇。已依提供的完整嵌入文字閱讀方法、結果、討論、限制、表格、圖說及可見補充材料說明；僅列出檔名而未提供內容的補充檔，不能視為已查核。全文讓組內變化與介入比較得以區分，也揭露部分摘要、正文與表格不一致，相關結論需保守保留並交由編輯確認。 
本週研究地圖 
本週所選研究集中於 Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition 的急性補充、體重管理、軍事體能與飲食工具，另有 Sports Health 的六季社區橄欖球腦震盪資料。共同進展是把營養、功能與健康放入具體族群，但證據沒有共同驗證一套上場或補充標準。咖啡因呈任務特異反應；橘皮素的體組成訊號較其有氧與肌力療效宣稱清楚；肉桂研究則受到報告不一致及無安慰劑設計限制。 
補充效益取決於任務與比較方式

決策前必懂的背景 
先釐清量測代表的構念，再決定是否改變策略。補充品試驗的效果需要比較條件，體組成需要核對工具與水合條件，回場紀錄需要區分參與、競賽及表現；本期沒有跨族群通用的進階切點。 
組內變化與組別 × 時間交互作用 
組內變化描述一組前後是否改變；交互作用檢驗各組變化模式是否不同。 
介入組顯著、對照組不顯著，仍不能單憑此推論介入優於對照。橘皮素的有氧結果尤其需要這項區分。 
cross-source-synthesis 
實驗室能力與競賽表現 
跳躍、閉鎖鏈推離與固定速度關節力矩，測量特定身體能力；競賽還包含技術、協調與情境。 
咖啡因提高 CMJ 或 BPU，不能直接寫成出拳速度、打擊力或勝率提高。 
source-stated 
典型誤差與個人反應 
典型誤差反映重複量測的波動；單次超過探索性門檻，仍不表示同一人會穩定受益。 
保留原始單位並重複核對；不依一次測試標記真正反應者，也不把研究的探索分類當臨床切點。 
表面效度、內容效度與效標效度 
表面效度關乎使用者是否覺得工具合理易懂；內容效度關乎是否涵蓋應測內容；效標效度需要與適當參照比較。 
ADI-Can 的試用結果不能證明攝取量測準確，也不能把澳洲版信度直接算到加拿大版。 
回到參與、回到比賽、回到表現 
本報操作上將參與定為恢復部分運動活動，比賽定為重新進入賽場，表現定為恢復或超越傷前競技水準。 
課程支持回場與回到表現的區分；部分參與的紀錄方式是本報提案。橄欖球缺席結束並未證明已恢復傷前表現。 
edge-sport-proposal 
飲食品質與能量不足 
飲食品質整理食物選擇與習慣；運動相對能量不足涉及健康與運動需求，不能只由體重或一個飲食總分判定。 
體重下降時同時檢查飲食、功能與健康情境；補充品造成的短期數值改變不能排除 RED-S。 
咖啡因可能影響神經驅動，但本試驗沒有驗證路徑 
論文以腺苷受體拮抗、喚醒與自主神經驅動作可能背景；未量測咖啡因濃度、神經驅動或基因型。 
60 分鐘區塊效果較清楚，不代表每位選手此時達藥物峰值。 
代謝假說與功能療效之間仍有距離 
橘皮素討論引用 AMPK、GLUT4 與脂質代謝，肉桂研究討論 irisin 及相關訊號；本期人體資料未直接確認這些路徑造成表現改善。 
不以 irisin、血脂或荷爾蒙的方向代替任務測試，也不據此宣稱補充與訓練有確定協同作用。 
腦震盪缺席包含照護與制度因素 
橄欖球論文提出症狀、既往史及醫療可近性等可能解釋，但未直接驗證；当地最低 21 天回場政策亦影響缺席分布。 
缺席天數不能當作純生理恢復時間，也不能由性別推算個人回場日期。

Twelve Watts, and a Better Question 
Does a promising change help the task, the gut, and the person? 
Ying and Bing examine a small cycling trial of bicarbonate gel after prolonged riding, then connect its promise and limits with gastrointestinal measurement, supplement uncertainty, hypoxic sprinting, recovery therapy, sleep, school exercise, and alcohol craving. Their central question is what evidence would justify keeping a new strategy.

Interpret the cycling gel result within its population, comparison, task order, and uncertainty. 
Separate symptom scores and physiological markers from meaningful functional outcomes. 
Distinguish acute responses, long-term adaptations, exploratory findings, and mixed-design pooled estimates. 
Describe a practical comparison process while recognizing that the EDGE SPORT workflow is unvalidated. 
The written weekly report is the evidence source for this episode. Research findings and EDGE SPORT operational proposals are distinguished in the conversation.

Capsaicin analogue meta-analysis: https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2733576 
Hypoxic repeated sprint trial: https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsc.70244

A finish worth measuring 
The cycling comparison, its 12-watt result, and the limits of individual interpretation. 
What does a gut score mean? 
Symptom definitions, measurement consistency, and functional interference. 
More stimulus, better outcome? 
Capsaicin uncertainty and the distinction between sprint output and physiological burden. 
Recovery and readiness 
CRET markers and exploratory sleep findings need separate functional interpretation. 
Different people, different endpoints 
School fitness and short-term alcohol craving illustrate outcome and population specificity. 
A decision you can revisit 
An explicitly unvalidated comparison process and a concise practical recap. 
Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and I keep imagining a rider who's done everything carefully but still fades near the finish, wondering whether one more gel would help. This week we're asking what would make an added strategy worth keeping. 
warm 
I'm Bing, and you're listening to edgeSport4Podcast, spoken as Edge Sport for Podcast. That rider's question feels familiar because a promising average can sound very personal, especially when the headline offers twelve extra watts after a long ride. 
Exactly. But extra compared with what, and during which part of the ride? 
curious 
Compared with the same carbohydrate intake without bicarbonate. Eleven trained cyclists completed both conditions in a randomized crossover experiment, so each person supplied their own comparison, and they were already accustomed to substantial carbohydrate intake during exercise. 
clear 
That background matters. Both conditions provided eighty grams of carbohydrate per hour during three hours of riding, and the added gel supplied a specific bicarbonate formulation, so this tested an addition to established fueling rather than a rescue for inadequate carbohydrate. 
And the performance test came after that riding, some short sprints, and a two minute effort. In the twelve minute test, average power was 239 watts with carbohydrate alone and 251 with the added bicarbonate, which sounds like a useful finish. 
reflective 
The paired difference was twelve watts, with a confidence interval from three to twenty two watts. That's encouraging for this particular test, although both conditions remained below the unfatigued reference, so the gel didn't erase the effect of the preceding work. 
cautious 
So it helped one finish. Did the shorter efforts improve too? 
They didn't show a clear additional advantage. That keeps me from calling this a general power boost, and the fixed test order leaves another question open, because we can't separate prolonged riding tolerance from recovery after those preceding hard efforts or changes in pacing. 
That's also where durability needs a careful definition. It's how well output holds up after accumulated exercise, while physiological resilience concerns things like efficiency and maximal oxygen uptake, so a better power result doesn't establish that every underlying physiological determinant was protected. 
Right, and the blood buffering response doesn't give us a personal success threshold either. Bicarbonate and blood pH increased, but the bicarbonate increase wasn't significantly related to the performance gain, so would you call someone a nonresponder after one unsuccessful trial? 
I wouldn't. Three of eleven didn't improve, but without repeatability data that isn't a stable personal label. 
And even a real gain has to coexist with being able to eat and finish the task. Nobody reported severe or extreme gut symptoms under this study's definition, but these were familiarized riders with controlled diets, so how much reassurance should that give someone else? 
Some reassurance about those conditions, not a general safety promise. The gut measurement review makes the wording especially important because it found fifty different scales across 126 studies, and ninety two percent of studies didn't explain why they chose their tool. 
Those are study counts, not the percentage of athletes who had symptoms. 
Yes, and two scales numbered zero to ten can still measure different things. Choosing a numbered category differs from marking a position on a continuous line, while changing the wording can shift the question from symptom severity to comfort, frequency, or interference. 
Which means I'd want to hear what actually happened alongside the score. Did nausea appear at a particular feeding point, did the rider skip food, or did they slow down, because a combined total can hide those differences and lose the timing? 
I'd keep the symptom names, anchors, and recording times consistent. The review isn't a formal systematic assessment of measurement properties, and limited reliability evidence doesn't amount to full validation, so it doesn't establish a universal score that tells everyone when symptoms become unacceptable. 
That makes a supplement ranking feel premature. How does the capsaicin review fit here? 
It asks a different question about single doses of capsaicin analogues, compounds related to capsaicin. The analysis combined twenty one crossover trials involving 348 adults across several performance domains, and its overall standardized effect was 0.20, with a confidence interval from 0.07 to 0.33. 
So that's a small average expressed on a common statistical scale, rather than watts or seconds. The prediction interval ran from negative 0.36 to positive 0.77, which allows quite different results across study settings, including settings without benefit despite that positive average. 
And the authors rated overall certainty very low. Would a plausible mechanism change your recommendation? 
It would make the question interesting, but it wouldn't repair the evidence. Proposed pathways involving a receptor called TRPV1, calcium handling, and discomfort weren't directly tested in most trials, and adverse effects weren't assessed systematically enough to turn a dose curve into a safety guide. 
Then I'd want stronger task specific trials and better tolerance reporting before routine use. The predominantly male samples also limit interpretation for women, and different compounds can't be assumed equivalent, so this review and the cycling trial don't let us choose a winning supplement. 
Agreed. The same temptation appears in training when a bigger stimulus sounds automatically better. 
The low oxygen sprint study gives that temptation something concrete to work against. Sixteen highly trained sprinters completed seven cycling sprints lasting either ten or fifteen seconds, with thirty seconds of rest in both conditions, and the longer sprints produced lower average power. 
Across the seven sprints, average power was 6.85 watts per kilogram for ten seconds and 6.30 for fifteen seconds. That tells us about output rate rather than proving lower total mechanical work, and the longer condition also showed a greater decline across repetitions. 
Yet average heart rate wasn't clearly different, while oxygen saturation measured shortly after each sprint was lower in the longer condition. So heart rate alone misses part of this comparison, and without a normal oxygen condition or long-term follow-up we can't declare the better training program. 
Exactly. And a recovery marker can miss the outcome we care about too. 
You're thinking of CRET, the capacitive resistive electric transfer treatment added to massage. Twenty five athletes completed active and sham conditions after repeated hard cycling efforts, and because both conditions included massage, the comparison isolates the addition of active treatment rather than the value of massage itself. 
Yes. At sixty minutes, lactate was lower with active treatment by 0.70 millimoles per liter, with a reported confidence interval from 0.05 to 1.50, but does that justify saying the athletes had recovered faster or were ready for more work? 
No. Strength, perceived fatigue, and next day's cycling performance didn't show clear advantages. 
There were some ultrasound differences too, but those didn't directly measure tissue repair or glycogen restoration. I find the contrast with the gel trial helpful because better twelve minute output there accompanied higher postexercise lactate, so the direction of lactate alone doesn't settle performance or recovery. 
That makes me cautious about another shortcut, using a sleep questionnaire as a readiness verdict. In the exploratory analysis of 104 healthy adults, participants completed a demanding cognitive task or watched a neutral documentary before testing, while sleep quality and chronotype were examined as possible modifiers. 
And chronotype means someone's tendency toward earlier or later timing. There were some general differences in reported mental fatigue and sleepiness, but those aren't the same as differences in the response to the cognitive task, so did the analysis establish that sleep doesn't matter? 
It didn't. Most analyses found no clear modifying effect, but a continuous sleep score analysis showed a small cognitive signal, and testing conditions may have limited sleep differences, so I'd record sleep, mental fatigue, and sleepiness separately rather than dismissing what someone reports. 
That separation matters beyond adult testing. Can school fitness gains tell us how children feel? 
Not automatically. The Danish FIT FIRST 20 trial randomized thirty schools and followed a high intensity multisport program for about forty weeks, but the denominators deserve care because 1652 children were randomized while 1195 with parental consent entered the analysis. 
The program involved three forty minute sessions each week compared with usual physical education. The adjusted additional gain on a repeated shuttle running test was 54.90 meters, with a confidence interval from 8.35 to 101.40, so that's an advantage over the comparison group's change. 
Exactly, rather than simply how far the program group improved. Jumping and agility also favored the program, but psychological outcomes didn't show a distinctive benefit, and frequency, content, and intensity changed together, so schools can't identify one winning ingredient or assume fitness gains establish psychological gains. 
Which brings us to a study where the reported endpoint actually was subjective, alcohol craving after brief exercise. Six articles suggested a short-term reduction, but the review combined controlled comparisons, before and after results, and natural activity observations, so what should we make of its pooled number? 
Carefully. It reported an approximate standardized effect of 0.55, with an approximate confidence interval from 0.40 to 0.80, but that's neither a percentage reduction in drinking nor a clean estimate from comparable randomized trials, and the claimed young adult focus doesn't match several middle-aged samples. 
So a short-term craving signal doesn't establish sustained drinking reduction or relapse prevention. 
Right, and it doesn't establish exercise as a way to manage withdrawal. It could inform discussion of an activity option within professional care, but I'd want clearer populations, consistent comparisons, and actual drinking outcomes before making a stronger claim about who benefits or for how long. 
That returns us to our rider, because the useful question is what would change a decision. Our EDGE SPORT proposal is to choose the relevant fatigued task beforehand, keep the existing fueling background comparable, and record output alongside individual symptoms, actual intake, and willingness to continue. 
encouraging 
I'd add repeated observations and the inconvenient results too, including trials with no gain or more discomfort. That's an unvalidated operational proposal rather than a tested package, but it makes the next discussion more concrete, especially if equipment, prior work, timing, or expectations differed. 
Then keep a strategy only when comparable observations support the person's goal and its burden is acceptable. If symptoms interfere with fueling or completion, pause the addition and review it with the team, because these studies don't supply a universal dose, success margin, or symptom cutoff. 
And don't let a reassuring heart rate, lower lactate, or better image make that decision alone. Read the written weekly report and original sources for methods and limitations, then bring the specific task and your actual experience into the conversation, because twelve watts is an invitation to investigate. 
Eleven trained cyclists compared the same 80 g/h carbohydrate background with and without a specific bicarbonate gel during 180 minutes of riding. 
Randomized crossover experiment with incomplete blinding. Participants were accustomed to high carbohydrate intake. The exposure is a study protocol, not a universal prescription. 
Fatigued twelve minute power averaged 239 W with carbohydrate and 251 W with added bicarbonate. The paired difference was 12 W with 95% CI 3–22 W. 
Testing followed three hours of riding and preceding short high intensity tasks. Both conditions remained below the unfatigued reference. Shorter tasks did not show a clear additional advantage. 
Three of eleven cyclists did not improve twelve minute performance. Bicarbonate increases were not significantly correlated with performance improvement. 
No protocol-specific repeatability evidence establishes stable individual responder classifications or a biochemical success threshold. 
No participant reported severe or extreme gastrointestinal symptoms under the cycling trial's definition. 
Small familiarized sample with controlled diets and limited symptom-tool validation. This does not establish general safety or superiority over other formulations. 
The gastrointestinal review included 126 studies using 50 scales. Ninety two percent did not explain tool selection. 
These are study-level descriptions, not symptom prevalence. The review was not a formal systematic assessment of measurement properties and established no universal severity cutoff. 
The capsaicin analogue analysis included 21 crossover trials and 348 adults. Overall g was 0.20 with 95% CI 0.07–0.33 and prediction interval −0.36 to 0.77. 
Overall certainty was very low. Predominantly male samples, heterogeneous compounds and tasks, and incomplete adverse-effect assessment prevent routine recommendations, dose equivalence, or supplement rankings. 
Sixteen highly trained sprinters completed seven ten or fifteen second cycling sprints in hypoxia with thirty seconds of rest. Average power was 6.85 and 6.30 W/kg respectively. 
Lower average power does not establish lower total mechanical work. The acute pilot study had no normoxic comparison or long-term adaptation follow-up. 
Longer hypoxic sprints produced lower sampled post-sprint oxygen saturation without a clear average heart-rate difference. 
Oxygen saturation was sampled about ten seconds after each sprint, not continuously. The result establishes neither a universal stopping threshold nor an optimal training program. 
In 25 athletes, active CRET added to massage lowered sixty minute lactate by a reported 0.70 mmol/L compared with sham plus massage, with 95% CI 0.05–1.50. 
Difference direction is sham minus active. Strength, perceived fatigue, and next-day Wingate performance showed no clear advantage. Absence of significance does not establish equivalence. Table and inference labels require editorial review. 
The exploratory sleep analysis involved 104 healthy adults. Most analyses did not detect clear modification of the mental fatigue response, while continuous sleep scores showed a small cognitive signal. 
Secondary hypotheses were not preregistered and exploratory multiplicity was uncontrolled. General subjective differences differ from response interactions. Findings do not establish that sleep is unimportant. 
The school trial randomized 1652 children across thirty schools and analyzed 1195 with parental consent. After about forty weeks, the adjusted additional shuttle-test gain was 54.90 m with 95% CI 8.35–101.40 m. 
The estimate is a group-by-time difference, not an intervention group's raw gain. Frequency, content, and intensity changed together. Psychological outcomes showed no intervention-specific advantage. 
Six articles on brief exercise and alcohol craving reported approximate g 0.55 with approximate 95% CI 0.40–0.80. 
Mixed comparison structures and age inconsistencies limit interpretation. This is not a drinking reduction percentage or proof of withdrawal safety, sustained drinking reduction, or relapse prevention. 
Match an added strategy to a specific task and a comparable existing fueling background. 
Record individual symptoms, their timing, and interference with feeding or task completion. 
Interpret heart rate, lactate, imaging, and questionnaires alongside actual function. 
Repeated comparisons and joint review are an unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal, without universal doses or decision thresholds. 
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for methods and limitations.

疲勞後多出 12 W：自行車補給效益如何通過腸胃與功能檢驗？ 
本週最具體的補給進展，是小型自行車交叉試驗中，運動期間加入碳酸氫鹽凝膠，改善長時間騎乘後的 12 分鐘計時測試；但短衝刺、2 分鐘測試及個人反應並未一致受益。腸胃量表綜述、低氧衝刺與恢復研究共同提醒：症狀分數、心率、乳酸或影像改變，都需要與實際功能及量測條件一起判讀。 
已習慣運動中補給的自行車選手，如何判斷新增補給策略是否改善疲勞後輸出，同時維持腸胃耐受與可比較的監測？ 
本期共 8 篇：full-text-open 8 篇，full-text-web、full-text-local、full-text-excerpt 與 abstract-only 各 0 篇；已閱讀提供的完整嵌入文字，包括方法、結果、討論、限制、表格、圖說及可用補充說明。全文可支持情境化判讀，但未附出的補充檔內部資料仍不可推定；部分文章存在摘要、正文或表格不一致，需人工編輯查核。完整取用不等於高確定性，尤其小樣本、探索分析與量表驗證不足會限制處方化。 
本週研究地圖 
本週 JISSN 聚焦補充品效果與腸胃量測品質；Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 同時新增疲勞狀態自行車補給及約 40 週校園體育介入資料；European Journal of Sport Science 則涵蓋低氧衝刺、恢復療法、心理疲勞與酒精渴求。研究並非互相直接驗證，但一致要求區分目標結果：體能改善未必伴隨心理改善，生理指標改變未必代表功能恢復，單次效益也未建立長期適應或疾病治療效果。 
補給效益取決於任務與證據品質 
pmid-42788859 
pmid-42816054 
碳酸氫鹽凝膠在疲勞後 12 分鐘自行車測試有額外效益；辣椒素類似物整合效果小，且作者評定整體證據確定性極低。兩者成分、任務與分析尺度不同，不能排名。

pmid-42811668 
pmid-42733310 
pmid-42723148 
腸胃量表缺乏一致驗證；CRET 的乳酸與影像差異未伴隨明確功能優勢；睡眠品質與時型的主觀差異也未穩定轉成心理疲勞反應差異。

增加刺激未必增加輸出或全面受益

pmid-42813573 
固定休息下延長低氧衝刺，功率下降且衝刺後 SpO2 較低；校園多運動課程改善部分體能，但未檢出介入特有心理效益。兩篇分別回答急性刺激與長期課程問題。 
短時間運動與酒精渴求的早期訊號 
pmid-42806437

12 W；95% CI 3–22 W 
疲勞後 12 分鐘計時測試的配對功率差 
11 名已訓練自行車選手，3 小時騎乘後；碳水加碳酸氫鹽相較相同碳水補給。 
126 篇研究、50 種量表 
運動腸胃量測的異質性 
健康成人運動研究的系統性與批判性綜述；不是量測性質的正式系統性評估。 
g = 0.20；95% CI 0.07–0.33 
辣椒素類似物的整體標準化效果 
21 項交叉試驗、348 名參與者、67 個效果值；預測區間 −0.36 至 0.77，整體 GRADE 極低。 
6.85 與 6.30 W/kg 
低氧重複衝刺平均功率 
16 名高度訓練短跑選手，7 趟 10 秒與 15 秒自行車衝刺，均休息 30 秒；數值為跨七趟平均。

丹麥校園叢集試驗，約 40 週後 YYIR1C 的組別與時間交互作用；1195 名具家長同意的分析樣本。 
0.70 mmol/L；95% CI 0.05–1.50 
CRET 主要乳酸結果 
25 名運動員，運動後 60 分鐘；差值方向為假 CRET 加按摩減主動 CRET 加按摩。 
決策前必懂的背景 
本期實務重點是疲勞後補給評估。先區分外部輸出、內部反應及量測誤差，再討論新增策略；單次試驗不能直接回答長期適應、安全上限或個人必然受益。 
疲勞耐受性（durability） 
累積運動後，功率或速度表現維持的程度。 
需比較相同任務在未疲勞及累積工作後的輸出，不能只用新鮮狀態測試推估比賽後段能力。 
source-stated 
生理韌性（physiological resilience） 
累積工作後，最大攝氧量、效率等生理表現決定因子維持的程度。 
生理韌性與外部功率耐受性相關但操作定義不同；本期凝膠研究不能證明所有生理決定因子均被保護。 
腸胃症狀發生、嚴重度與功能影響 
發生指是否出現，嚴重度指主觀程度，功能影響指是否妨礙補給、運動或完成任務。 
分別記錄個別症狀、出現時間與任務干擾；總分相同不代表症狀或影響相同。 
Likert 類別評分與 VAS 
前者選擇離散等級，通常產生序位資料；後者在連續線段上標記程度。 
固定格式、文字錨點與量測時點，不能因都標成 0–10 就視為可互換，也不能直接套用別篇的嚴重度分界。 
信度與效度 
信度關注重測的一致性；效度關注工具是否測到目標構念並適合用途。 
重測可靠不等於已全面驗證，也不代表已建立可用於運動中決策的分數門檻。 
心理疲勞與嗜睡 
心理疲勞是持續高認知需求後的心理生理狀態；嗜睡是睡意與警醒程度的主觀表現。 
分開詢問與量測，避免把睡眠問卷分數當作當日心理疲勞或體能輸出的替代值。 
急性反應與長期適應 
急性反應發生於當次刺激及短期恢復；長期適應是持續訓練後較持久的改變。 
補給、低氧衝刺及恢復療法的單次結果，不能直接推導長期訓練效果。 
inclass-supported 
生理標記與功能恢復 
乳酸、超音波或氧飽和度描述部分生理狀態；功能恢復描述力量與任務能力是否恢復。 
兩類結果並列判讀，不能因標記改善就自動增加下一次負荷。 
cross-source-synthesis 
細胞外緩衝是合理解釋，尚非個人受益門檻 
碳酸氫鹽補給提高血液 HCO3− 與 pH，作者提出有助高強度運動的酸鹼緩衝；但本試驗中 HCO3− 增幅與表現增益的相關未達顯著，不能建立通關濃度。 
以疲勞後任務表現及耐受為決策核心，生化資料作為補充。 
更長衝刺與固定休息可能改變恢復需求 
低氧研究中延長衝刺降低平均功率及衝刺後 SpO2；PCr 恢復受限與代謝負擔是作者提出的可能機轉，但未直接量測。 
不能只以心率相近判定兩種課表刺激相同，亦不能把較大急性負擔當成較佳長期適應。 
乳酸濃度方向沒有單一表現意義 
凝膠試驗中較佳 12 分鐘表現伴隨較高運動後乳酸；CRET 試驗中較低 60 分鐘乳酸未伴隨功能優勢。兩者情境不同，顯示濃度需依產生、交換與取樣時點解讀。 
不以乳酸高低單獨決定疲勞程度或恢復完成。 
TRPV1 路徑仍屬補充品效果的機轉假說 
辣椒素綜述提出 TRPV1、鈣離子處理與不適感調節可能影響表現，但多數納入試驗未直接驗證中介機轉。 
機轉合理性不能補足極低確定性，也不能證明不同化合物可用相同劑量替代。 
nutrition 
training 
monitoring 
assessment 
performance 
sport-medicine 
從指標變化走向任務效益與量測品質 
延續第 38–40 週的情境化監測，本週更具體地把補給與恢復判讀放到疲勞後任務：有平均效益時仍要查個人反應，沒有功能差異時不能靠乳酸或影像替策略背書。腸胃量表綜述也修正了把常用分數視為已驗證標準的習慣；目前適合建立可回顧的評估流程，尚不足以制定跨運動、跨族群的通用進階門檻。 
full-text-open 
未前瞻註冊的系統性與批判性綜述；不是量測性質的正式系統性綜述。 
126 篇研究、共 3540 名參與者；每篇 6–272 人，納入設定為健康成人 ≥18 歲，涵蓋不同訓練程度與性別，以跑步及自行車為主。 
運動前、中、後使用的腸胃症狀量表、症狀用語、錨點、分類與分析方式。 
比較不同研究的量測做法，無統一介入對照。 
量表種類與長度、選擇理由、驗證與信度證據、取樣及統計報告方式。 
搜尋於 2025 年 8 月進行，無出版年份限制；原研究量測時程不同，無共同追蹤期。 
工具異質性 
126 篇研究使用 50 種量表、13 種量表長度；92% 未說明選擇理由。 
研究層級描述，非參與者症狀發生率。 
摘要、結果 3.2 與結論 
運動與場景分布 
跑步 68 篇、自行車 39 篇；研究特徵段列實驗室 96 篇、場域 30 篇。 
126 篇納入研究；後續取樣段另列實驗室 95 篇及一篇開放式量測，需核對。 
結果 3.1、3.2 
重測一致性邊界 
討論引用 mVAS 總症狀分數的 95% 一致性界限，最佳情境約 ±25、最差約 ±95 分。 
來自所引用信度研究的累積總分；不是單一 0–10 症狀分數，也不是本綜述建立的臨床門檻。 
討論 4.1 
腸胃分數先確認工具與用語，再談嚴重度 
運動腸胃量測存在大量格式與分類差異。常見 0–10 工具的重測資料不等於全面效度驗證，慢性跑者回溯問卷也不能直接證明適合運動中使用；本篇提供方法框架，而非新的有效嚴重度切點。 
只有一項研究評估運動特定 11 點工具的信度，另有一项跑者慢性症狀回溯問卷的驗證資料。 
症狀、舒適感、頻率與功能干擾是不同構念，改寫錨點可能改變測量內容。 
累積總分會降低時間解析度，宜補充個別症狀及個人反應。 
延伸課程的科學化監測，新增對工具構念與驗證狀態的檢查；相較第 39 週的腸胃演練，本篇要求先確認耐受結果如何被量測，沒有直接比較補給療效。

course-3508b0d2cc8ec57d 
在監测方法层次延伸課程的客觀評估與系統化規劃；未驗證棒球握力或負荷工具，也不能將其門檻移用於腸胃症狀。 
2026-w39 
支持第 39 週補給需檢驗個人耐受的方向，並增加量表一致性與功能干擾記錄；不是對自行車營養聲明效果的直接驗證。

中高齡女性開始重訓：加蛋白質、加肌酸或加有氧，如何判斷下一步？ 
力量、肌肉量與心肺適能需要不同證據。以中高齡女性訓練與蛋白質試驗，對照成人肌酸統合分析，本專題建立「先確認訓練刺激與飲食，再評估營養加成」的執行流程，釐清未檢出差異、體組成估計及女性證據不足的決策邊界。 
training 
nutrition 
assessment 
monitoring 
對剛開始阻力訓練、以增加力量為主要目標的中高齡女性，何時應先調整訓練與飲食執行，何時才值得討論提高蛋白質或加入肌酸？ 
兩篇全文回答不同但相連的問題：女性隨機試驗比較阻力訓練後增加騎車，以及不同蛋白質目標的飲食諮詢；肌酸統合分析比較阻力訓練加肌酸與加安慰劑。可以整合成決策流程，不能將兩篇效果值直接排名，也不能推論肌酸優於蛋白質，或能抵銷新增有氧後的力量差距。已依所附全文、表格、圖說、討論及限制判讀；未附的補充檔不視為已核閱。 
封包中的 2026 年 9 月肌酸研究與 ACSM 女性能量平衡更新，使「營養如何支持訓練」成為適合深入說明的問題。更新題名只提供時效背景；效果與數值全部取自本期選定全文。 
第 39 週已介紹新增騎車的結果取捨，第 40 週已介紹肌酸平均效益；仍缺少以中高齡女性為主體、能區分訓練不足、飲食未落實與可考慮補充情境的完整流程。尤其女性試驗的蛋白質不顯著結果，容易被誤讀成不必重視蛋白質。 
當力量進步不如預期，團隊需決定要維持方案、調整新增騎車、修正飲食，或另行試用肌酸；同時避免以 BIA 肌肉量上升、體脂率下降或補充品用量，代替真正的能力結果。 
區分力量表現、BIA 骨骼肌量、瘦體重與體脂率，說明各自能支持的結論。 
讀懂第 12 週調整後組間差、Hedges’ g、信賴區間與預測區間。 
說明蛋白質指派目標未檢出差異，為何不代表三種攝取量等效。 
辨認成人肌酸整合結果外推到中高齡女性時的限制。 
完成包含基線、分期課表、飲食紀錄、選擇性補充、進退階與複評責任人的執行方案。 
先問希望改善哪個結果，再問目前實際做了什麼。肌肉量是組織或儀器估計，力量是完成特定任務的能力，有氧適能又是另一個面向。營養介入能否提供額外效益，取決於比較條件、實際攝取及訓練背景；不能由單一研究的顯著或不顯著結果，直接決定所有人的飲食。 
阻力訓練與並行訓練 
阻力訓練（RT）以外在阻力安排肌肉工作；本期並行訓練（CT）是在相同的全身阻力課表後，立即增加自行車訓練。 
CT 的總時間及運動暴露較多。試驗比較的是增加騎車的整套安排，沒有隔離等時間、等工作量下的純訓練模式差異。 
source-stated 
指派蛋白質目標與實際攝取 
指派目標是營養諮詢要求達成的攝取量；實際攝取是參與者真正吃進的量。本試驗以自陳飲食紀錄估計後者。 
平均紀錄接近目標，仍不能證明每日精確達標；也不能把自由生活、非等熱量的飲食諮詢，解讀為隔離蛋白質本身的劑量試驗。 
骨骼肌量、瘦體重與肌肥大 
女性試驗的骨骼肌量由 BIA 模型估計；肌酸統合分析的瘦體重包含水分及其他非脂肪組織。肌肥大則涉及肌肉組織大小的增加。 
兩篇的體組成結果並非同一測量，不能直接互換。水分分布、前置條件與儀器誤差都會影響解讀；瘦體重增加不能全部算成新生肌肉。 
cross-source-synthesis 
估計 1-RM 與估計 VO₂max 
女性試驗以負重與完成次數推估最大肌力，並以次最大騎車心率反應推估最大攝氧量。 
沒有直接完成最大重量或量測呼吸氣體。動作熟悉度、騎車經濟性與心率反應可能影響估計結果。 
調整後組間差與組內變化 
調整後組間差比較基線校正後兩條件的第 12 週結果；組內變化則比較同組前後的原始數值。 
CT − RT 為負，不代表 CT 自己下降。女性試驗所有組別原始平均體重都上升，仍可同時出現 CT 的調整後體重低於 RT。 
Hedges’ g、95% CI 與 95% PI 
肌酸研究的 g 是兩組前後變化差異的標準化效果；CI 描述平均效果估計的不確定性，PI 描述未來研究情境可能出現的效果範圍。 
g = 0.55 不是增加 0.55 kg 或改善 55%。平均效果的 CI 不跨零，仍可能伴隨跨零的 PI；兩者回答不同問題。 
未檢出差異與等效 
未檢出差異表示現有設計與資料未提供足夠證據確認差異；等效需要預先界定可接受差異範圍並以合適設計檢驗。 
兩篇都沒有由不顯著結果證明不同營養劑量可互換。女性試驗的檢定力主要針對中至大型交互作用，較小差異仍可能存在。 
肌酸可能增加高強度工作的供能餘裕 
肌酸全文以磷酸肌酸支持快速 ATP 再合成、增加可完成的高強度訓練，以及細胞水合等途徑解釋力量與瘦體重結果。這些是論文討論的機轉背景，統合分析未一致測量完整的中介路徑。 
【cross-source-synthesis】補充後仍需確認是否實際完成更多或更高品質的訓練，以及力量是否改變；不能只用體重增加推定機轉已奏效。 
pmid-42765482 
額外騎車同時改變刺激、時間與恢復需求 
女性試驗的 CT 在重訓後增加騎車，力量測驗較偏向 RT，有氧估計值較偏向 CT。累積疲勞、實際阻力刺激、恢復與測驗特異性都可能參與，但研究沒有直接測量分子或神經肌肉干擾。 
【cross-source-synthesis】力量落後時先查新增騎車與重訓完成量，不把差距自動歸因於蛋白質不足，也不宣稱有氧必然妨礙所有肌肉適應。 
pmid-42735207 
體脂率下降可能來自分母改變 
肌酸統合分析中瘦體重增加、脂肪量未檢出差異，而體脂率略降；作者認為非脂肪部分增加可解釋比例變化。由於水分未被分別統合，無法確定組織與水分各自的貢獻。 
【cross-source-synthesis】同時呈現體重、脂肪量或體脂率、測量條件及力量，不將較低體脂率直接標示為減脂成功。 
83/108 人；流失 23.1% 
女性試驗的實際分析樣本 
40–77 歲女性隨機分派後，83 人完成第 12 週所有結果評估；採完整案例分析，沒有完整意向治療估計。 
−6.68 kg；95% CI −8.32 至 −5.04 
新增騎車條件的腿推估計 1-RM 較低 
第 12 週基線調整後 CT − RT，合併三種蛋白質指派；Holm 調整後 p < 0.001。不是 CT 組自己減少的重量。 
4.53 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹；95% CI 3.80–5.25 
新增騎車條件的有氧估計值較高 
第 12 週調整後 CT − RT；Ekblom–Bak 次最大自行車測驗推估，沒有呼吸氣體量測；Holm 調整後 p < 0.001。 
0.8、1.6、2.2 g·kg⁻¹·日⁻¹ 
試驗指派的蛋白質目標 
以實際體重計算並每週更新，屬自由生活飲食諮詢條件；主要骨骼肌量結果的蛋白質主效應 p = 0.726，不能據此判定等效或最佳攝取量。 
63 項試驗；1,489 人；女性 248 人 
肌酸統合分析的規模與女性代表性 
作者報告男性 970 人、女性 248 人、未報性別 271 人；18–75 歲，各結果使用不同研究子集，人數不可跨結果加總。 
g = 0.55；95% CI 0.38–0.71；95% PI −0.04–1.14 
肌酸的下肢肌力平均加成 
阻力訓練加肌酸相對加安慰劑；排除一個離群效果值後的三層模型。預測區間跨零，不保證每個情境受益。 
單中心、12 週、平行組隨機 2 × 3 因子試驗；依基線骨骼肌量分層，以密封信封隱藏分派，結果評估者盲化。主要推論採基線調整 ANCOVA，分析限 83 位完整案例。

沒有直接比較提高蛋白質與加入肌酸，也沒有驗證兩者合用在中高齡女性的加成或交互作用。

BIA 與瘦體重中的水分、其他非脂肪組織及真正肌肥大各占多少，未能確認。 
研究不能直接代表衰弱、已確診肌少症、心血管疾病、術後或高水平女性運動員；停經階段亦未得到充分處理。

A Change Worth Acting On? 
Creatine, confidence after ACL reconstruction, and what a spine screening score can tell us 
Ying and Bing explore when a measurement should change a training decision. They discuss adult creatine trials, physiotherapists' experiences of psychological support after ACL reconstruction, and spine screening in adolescent rhythmic gymnasts, keeping average effects, professional experience, and screening associations distinct.

Interpret standardized strength effects without converting them into personal guarantees. 
Distinguish lean mass, fat mass, and body fat percentage. 
Explain what physiotherapist focus groups can contribute to ACL rehabilitation decisions. 
Distinguish spine screening categories from diagnoses and causal evidence. 
Identify what additional information could support maintaining training, progressing a task, or arranging professional assessment. 
Pronounce edgeSport4Podcast as Edge Sport for Podcast. The digit 4 means for. 
All research content comes from weeklyReport 2026-w40. No relatedIssues evidence is used. 
Creatine source: Resistance training combined with creatine supplementation: a three-level meta-analysis of multidimensional outcomes from strength enhancement to body composition remodeling. https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2718316 
ACL source: From Fear to Function: How Physiotherapists Navigate Psychological Challenges in Patients Undergoing Rehabilitation After ACL Reconstruction. https://doi.org/10.1177/19417381261471381 
Gymnastics source: Risk of Scoliosis in Adolescent Female Rhythmic Gymnasts Compared with Healthy Peers: A Cross-Sectional Study Using the Scoliosis Tele-Screening Test. https://doi.org/10.1177/19417381261485714 
The creatine appendix was unavailable in the supplied evidence. Outcome-specific GRADE details and individual study characteristics require verification. 
The gymnastics paper contains inconsistencies in category percentages, the precise STS-Test P value, and BMI reporting. This script retains reported counts and means. 
The closing decision workflow is an EDGE SPORT operational proposal. The three studies did not validate it as a combined intervention. 
When a number asks for a decision 
The week's central question and the different kinds of evidence available. 
Creatine and the meaning of improvement 
Average strength effects, uncertainty, body composition, and individual relevance. 
Making room for fear in rehabilitation 
What experienced physiotherapists describe and what remains untested. 
A screening result needs interpretation 
Rhythmic gymnastics findings without diagnostic or causal overreach. 
What would change the next step? 
An explicitly unvalidated proposal for documenting decisions and follow-up. 
Welcome to edgeSport4Podcast. I'm Ying, and imagine sitting with your coffee and a training report that looks better than last month's. Before you celebrate or change the plan, what does that improvement actually give you permission to do? 
warm 
I'm Bing, and here on edgeSport4Podcast we're asking when a change is enough to act on. This week's report brings together strength gains, confidence after knee reconstruction, and spine screening, with very different evidence behind each. 
curious 
And the person looking at that report may want a simple answer. Should I keep going, try the next task, or get something checked? Our job today is to see which parts of those questions the research can actually answer. 
reflective 
Let's keep asking what was measured and whose experience it represents. That should make the practical answers more useful. 
clear 
The creatine paper gives us an actual intervention comparison. It pooled randomized trials of adults doing resistance training with creatine against adults doing resistance training with a placebo, so training was part of both sides of the comparison. 
That matters when someone credits everything to the supplement. The authors reported 63 trials and 1,489 adults overall, but different outcomes used different subsets of studies, so we shouldn't add the outcome sample sizes together. 
Before we give the strength result, what does the effect number mean for someone who usually thinks in kilograms? 
They used Hedges' g, which puts the difference in the groups' changes onto a standardized scale. That lets researchers combine different strength measurements, but a value of point five doesn't mean half a kilogram or a fifty percent improvement. 
On that scale, the upper body strength effect was point five four in favor of creatine. For lower body strength, the estimate was point five five after removing one outlying effect value, while the complete analysis gave point six six. 
So the average favors adding creatine, and removing that unusual value made the lower body estimate smaller. How certain is that average? 
For that lower body estimate, the ninety five percent confidence interval ran from point three eight to point seven one. That's uncertainty around the estimated average effect, but a coach also needs to ask how much results might vary across study settings. 
That's where the prediction interval helps. After removing the outlier, it ranged from minus point zero four to one point one four, crossing zero and leaving room for a future study setting with little or no benefit. 
cautious 
And that interval describes possible study effects, rather than giving an individual athlete their own predicted range of strength gains. 
Exactly, and publication bias is another reason to stay measured. A sensitivity analysis that modeled potentially missing effects reduced both strength estimates, although they remained positive. Those modeled effects weren't additional trials that researchers had actually conducted. 
I still find the average strength signal useful for a nutrition discussion. But suppose someone says their scan shows more lean mass and less body fat percentage, so creatine must have built muscle and burned fat. Would you accept both claims? 
I'd separate them. Lean mass increased on average, but lean mass includes water as well as other nonfat tissue, and this analysis couldn't separate those contributions. Calling all of that increase new muscle would go beyond the measurements. 
And a smaller fat percentage can happen when the total changes, even without a clear reduction in the amount of fat? 
Yes, that's the denominator changing. The analysis found a small decrease in body fat percentage but didn't detect a significant difference in fat mass, so it doesn't establish a fat loss benefit from adding creatine to training. 
Then I'd want to know whether the person is getting stronger in a way they value and how they feel about any weight change. Can this paper at least tell us which supplement schedule is most likely to deliver that? 
It didn't identify consistent effects of dose or supplementation schedule on the results. That leaves the best prescription unresolved, and it doesn't establish that all schedules work equally well. The authors rated overall evidence certainty from low to moderate. 
So there's enough to discuss a possible addition, but not enough to promise a particular person's response. 
And that discussion needs context. Women were less represented, diet and hydration reporting were incomplete, and the appendix wasn't available in the supplied evidence. For an individual decision, I'd want their training record, nutrition context, strength changes, and priorities alongside the average result. 
Those priorities become especially visible when someone is rebuilding confidence after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, usually called ACL reconstruction. Our next paper asks how physiotherapists handle psychological challenges during rehabilitation, which is a different question from whether a treatment improves outcomes. 
Different because we're listening to therapists describe their work, rather than following patients through a tested intervention? 
Yes, there were 21 physiotherapists across six focus groups, with 11 from the Netherlands and 10 from Norway. Researchers analyzed the discussions for themes, and there was no intervention comparison or patient follow-up measuring return to sport or reinjury. 
What I found useful was their description of a therapeutic alliance, meaning cooperation built around shared goals, agreed tasks, and trust. They described small achievable goals and gradually approaching feared movements as ways to connect physical progress with confidence. 
Would you call those strategies effective based on these interviews, or would that skip a step in the evidence? 
It would skip the patient's experience and the outcome testing. These are strategies therapists described using, not demonstrated improvements in return rates, though they give us concrete questions about which task feels frightening and whether the athlete feels supported. 
That last question feels easy to miss if the team believes it's already being supportive. The therapists also described group training as potentially helpful, but comparison with someone progressing faster could add pressure, so the same setting may be experienced differently. 
Then a better confidence score wouldn't settle everything. What would you still want to hear from the athlete? 
I'd ask which activity now feels manageable and which still doesn't, as a practical application of the report. The therapists used psychological questionnaires inconsistently, and some relied more on conversation, so this study gives us no universal score that clears someone to progress. 
I'd also ask whose timetable they're trying to meet. The interviews highlighted expectations from coaches, family, and teammates, along with limits in therapists' psychological training and access to referral services. Good intentions don't tell us whether needed support was actually available. 
And we should resist turning every interview example into homework. Some therapists mentioned injury footage or returning to the injury location, but the study didn't establish when those approaches are appropriate or whether they're safe and effective. 
Agreed. I'd use these findings to improve the conversation and clarify support needs, while keeping progression within the person's rehabilitation plan. I'd be more confident about prescribing a particular strategy if research included patient perspectives and measured patient outcomes. 
That wish for information we don't yet have carries into the gymnastics paper. It compared spine screening results in 56 female rhythmic gymnasts and 302 girls of similar age who didn't participate in sport, using a single assessment rather than following changes over time. 
Before the numbers, does a higher score mean more diagnosed scoliosis, or does it identify something that needs interpretation? 
It identifies screening risk. The Scoliosis Tele-Screening Test, or STS-Test, combines information such as family history, maturation, and visible asymmetry, so the total isn't simply a measure of spinal shape. This study didn't confirm scoliosis with imaging. 
With that distinction in place, the gymnasts averaged five point three four points, compared with three point four one in the comparison group. Those are points on the screening tool, and the group averages don't tell us each girl's classification. 
Where did the difference show up when they looked at the categories instead of just the average score? 
Mainly in the middle category. There were 35 gymnasts classified as medium risk out of 56, compared with 60 out of 302 in the comparison group. Keeping those denominators attached matters because the two groups were very different in size. 
And the high risk category didn't show a statistically significant group difference, which doesn't establish that the groups were equal. It also means we shouldn't describe every risk category as elevated or turn the medium risk counts into numbers of diagnosed cases. 
The training hours result is where I can imagine a coach wanting an immediate rule. Within the gymnast group, weekly hours and screening scores had a positive correlation of point four five six, meaning they tended to rise together. 
But we can't turn that association into an hourly ceiling, or assume reducing hours would lower the screening score. 
Right, the study can't establish what came first or separate training from selection and other influences. The girls had at least five years of gymnastics experience and were in competitive tiers three and four, so this isn't a sample of everyone attending a gymnastics class. 
Suppose a parent brings in a medium risk result and asks whether their daughter should stop training. I'd explain that the category needs clinical interpretation and isn't itself a stopping rule. What would help you make the next decision more concrete? 
I'd want the components behind the score, the maturation and training context, and a clinician's assessment of what follow-up is appropriate. The authors suggested screening every six months during growth, but their study didn't test that interval or show that it prevents progression. 
There's also some editorial checking still needed. The paper's percentages don't fully match its category counts, and there are inconsistencies in statistical reporting, so we've retained the reported counts and means without quietly correcting the source. 
That leaves a useful observation with a clear limit. To make stronger prevention decisions, we'd need follow-up connecting these screening results with later clinical outcomes, and evidence testing whether changes in training improve those outcomes. 
So here's our practical proposal from EDGE SPORT, and these studies haven't validated it as a combined process. Before changing training, write down what changed, what the measurement represents, what the athlete wants, and what unanswered question could change the decision. 
encouraging 
I'd add a named person and a date for reviewing the next step. That makes maintaining training, trying an agreed task, or arranging assessment something the team can revisit, without pretending we've discovered a universal progression threshold. 
For this week, discuss creatine through actual strength goals and body changes, ask about specific fears during ACL rehabilitation, and take spine screening concerns to clinical interpretation. Each asks for a different kind of follow-up, and none supplies an automatic personal clearance. 
And leave room for the athlete's answer to change the plan. You'll find the methods, numbers, and remaining uncertainties in the written weekly report and original sources. Thanks for joining us on edgeSport4Podcast, and we'll talk again next week. 
The creatine review reported 63 randomized trials and 1,489 adults, comparing resistance training plus creatine with resistance training plus placebo. 
Outcome analyses use different study subsets with overlapping participants. Their sample sizes must not be added together. This is adult evidence, not an adolescent or ACL-specific supplementation protocol. 
Upper body strength favored creatine with Hedges' g = 0.54, 95% CI 0.37–0.71. Lower body strength was g = 0.66 in the full analysis and g = 0.55 after excluding one outlying effect value. 
Hedges' g expresses standardized between-group differences in change, not kilograms or percentage improvement. Full and outlier-excluded estimates must remain distinguished. 
The outlier-excluded lower body strength estimate had a 95% confidence interval of 0.38–0.71 and a 95% prediction interval of −0.04–1.14. 
The confidence interval concerns uncertainty in the average effect. The prediction interval concerns effects in future study settings and is not an individual prediction interval. Both upper and lower body strength prediction intervals crossed zero. 
Publication-bias sensitivity analyses reduced strength estimates to g = 0.36 for upper body and g = 0.35 for lower body strength, with confidence intervals remaining above zero. 
Trim-and-fill models hypothetical missing effects rather than adding observed trials. This sensitivity analysis used a two-level method treating effects as independent. 
Lean mass increased with g = 0.30, 95% CI 0.18–0.41. Fat mass showed no statistically significant difference, g = −0.10, 95% CI −0.23–0.03, while body fat percentage decreased slightly, g = −0.14, 95% CI −0.26–−0.02. 
Lean mass includes water, and the analysis could not separate water from tissue contributions. A reduced fat percentage does not establish fat loss. Standardized effects are not kilograms or percentage points. 
The review did not identify consistent dose or supplementation-schedule moderation, and the authors rated overall certainty as low to moderate. 
Failure to detect moderation does not establish equivalent regimens or an optimal dose. Women were less represented, contextual reporting was incomplete, and the missing appendix prevents independent verification of detailed outcome-level GRADE assessments. 
The ACL study involved 21 physiotherapists in six focus groups, including 11 from the Netherlands and 10 from Norway. 
Participants were therapists recruited through professional networks, not patients. There was no intervention comparator or longitudinal patient outcome assessment. 
Therapists described trust, shared goals, small milestones, gradual exposure to feared movements, mixed experiences of group training, external pressure, and referral barriers. 
These are professional accounts, not demonstrated improvements in return to sport, reinjury, or patient experience. The study validates no psychological clearance threshold and does not establish injury footage or injury-site visits as safe required tasks. 
The gymnastics study compared 56 female rhythmic gymnasts with 302 similarly aged girls who did not participate in sport. Mean STS-Test scores were 5.34 ± 2.70 versus 3.41 ± 3.39 points. 
This was a single cross-sectional assessment without imaging-confirmed scoliosis. Gymnasts had at least five years of experience and were in tiers 3 and 4. Findings should not be generalized to all gymnastics participants. 
Medium risk counts were 35 of 56 gymnasts and 60 of 302 controls. High risk counts were 2 and 16, respectively, with no statistically significant high risk category difference. 
Counts describe screening categories, not diagnosed cases. A nonsignificant difference does not establish equality. Reported gymnast percentages conflict with counts, so the script uses counts without deriving replacement percentages. 
Weekly training hours correlated with STS-Test scores within the gymnast group, Spearman r = 0.456, P = 0.01. 
The association establishes neither causation nor a safe hourly limit. It does not show that reducing hours lowers scores or prevents disease. 
The gymnastics authors suggested screening every six months during growth. 
The study did not test that interval, longitudinal progression, or the effectiveness of screening-linked interventions. Clinical interpretation is required rather than automatic training cessation based on a category. 
Interpret creatine benefits alongside actual training, strength goals, and body changes. 
Ask about specific feared tasks and perceived support during ACL rehabilitation. 
Treat STS-Test results as screening information requiring interpretation, not diagnoses or automatic stopping rules. 
Record the next step, responsible person, and review date as an explicitly unvalidated EDGE SPORT proposal. 
Consult the written weekly report and original sources for full methods and limitations. 
The speech is synthetic. Ying is locally generated from the supplied female-voice sample, and Bing is locally generated from the supplied male-voice sample. The script is prepared by Codex. This episode is educational and does not provide individualized medical advice or return-to-play clearance.

本週三篇全文分別提供肌酸輔助阻力訓練的效果整合、ACL 重建復健的心理支持經驗，以及青少女韻律體操的脊椎側彎風險篩檢資料。實務上的共同問題是辨認量測代表什麼：瘦體重增加不能全部視為肌肉增生，治療師經驗不能當成療效驗證，篩檢分數也不能取代診斷。 
當肌力、心理準備或脊椎篩檢結果改變時，團隊如何決定維持訓練、分級進階或啟動專業評估？ 
本期包含 3 篇 full-text-open；full-text-web、full-text-local、full-text-excerpt 與 abstract-only 均為 0 篇。已閱讀所附完整文字中的方法、結果、討論、限制、表格、圖說與可見補充說明；肌酸論文提及的 Appendix.docx 未附實際內容，因此不能獨立核對附錄逐篇資料與各結果的 GRADE 細節。三篇分別為隨機試驗統合分析、質性焦點團體研究及橫斷面研究，能支持的效果、經驗與關聯推論須分開處理。

心理準備與治療聯盟 
心理準備涉及重返運動的認知判斷、情緒及行為準備；治療聯盟是患者與治療師基於共同目標、任務及信任建立的合作關係。 
量表之外，須了解害怕的具体任務、外界壓力與患者對支持的感受；治療師自認支持充分不代表患者也如此感受。

STS-Test 整合病史、成熟狀態及外觀不對稱等項目，用來辨識風險；本研究沒有以影像確診脊椎側彎。 
女性分類為低風險 0–4 分、中風險 5–11 分、高風險 12–15 分。這些是工具分類，並非停訓、手術或確診門檻。 
軀幹旋轉角與全身性關節過度活動 
ATR 是前彎時以脊椎側彎量角器量測的軀幹旋轉角；Beighton 分數評估關節過度活動，本研究採 ≥6/9 分分類。 
ATR 不等同影像 Cobb 角；Beighton 分數也不能單獨判定脊椎側彎或限制運動。

將心理反應放入每次訓練討論；目前仍屬治療師經驗，不能宣稱已確認作用機制或療效。

體操選手較常落在篩檢中風險類別，尚不能稱為側彎確診率較高 
女性韻律體操選手的 STS-Test 平均分數較高，分類差異主要由中風險較多、低風險較少所構成。每週時數與分數正相關，支持在生長期間留意風險訊號；研究未確診側彎，也未證明訓練時數造成疾病或減量能預防進展。 
高風險類別未見顯著組間差異，不能把整體結果概括為所有風險層級都較高。 
STS-Test 含家族史、性別及月經成熟資訊，分數並非單純反映脊椎外觀或角度。

What Would Support the Next Step? 
Fuel, training tradeoffs, and what returning to sport really tells us 
Ying and Bing discuss cycling nutrition guidance, a randomized training and protein trial in middle-aged and older women, and a hip surgery case series. Together they examine what was recommended, what actually happened, and whether the measured outcome answers the athlete's real question.

Distinguish a nutrition position statement, a randomized trial, and a retrospective case series. 
Interpret assigned nutrition targets separately from actual intake and training exposure.
